people.name: Dr. Priya Ramanathan
people.bio: Priya completed her PhD in Applied Mathematics at Imperial College London, where she developed novel topological methods for analysing high-dimensional sensory data. Before joining the programme, she held a postdoctoral position at ETH Zürich working on persistent homology applications in chemical informatics. She leads the FlavorSpace project and is passionate about bridging pure mathematics with real-world taste perception challenges.
people.researchDescription: Priya's research sits at the intersection of topological data analysis and sensory science. She uses persistent homology and mapper algorithms to build low-dimensional representations of flavour perception that capture the nonlinear structure of human taste. Her current focus is on developing computational frameworks that can predict how novel ingredient combinations will be perceived, with applications in rational flavour design and food product development.

equipment.name: Sensory Evaluation Suite (12-booth)
equipment.description: ISO-compliant individual tasting booths with controlled lighting and ventilation

people.name: Dr. Tomás Eriksson
people.bio: Tomás earned his PhD in Computer Science from KTH Royal Institute of Technology in Stockholm, specialising in knowledge representation and natural language understanding. He spent two years at a food-tech startup in Berlin building recipe recommendation engines before joining the programme. He leads the RecipeGraph project and contributes to cross-programme data infrastructure.
people.researchDescription: Tomás works on computational representations of culinary knowledge, building knowledge graphs that encode relationships between ingredients, techniques, flavour compounds, and cultural contexts. His research combines natural language processing with structured ontologies to enable machines to reason about food in ways that reflect human culinary intuition. He is particularly interested in how AI can generate novel but culturally coherent recipes.

people.name: Dr. Mei-Ling Zhao
people.bio: Mei-Ling holds a PhD in Biochemical Engineering from Tsinghua University and completed postdoctoral training at the Technical University of Denmark in industrial fermentation. Her expertise spans microbial ecology, metabolomics, and bioprocess control. She leads the Fermentation Whisperer project and co-supervises two PhD students working on fermentation-related topics.
people.researchDescription: Mei-Ling's research focuses on using machine learning to predict and control the complex microbial dynamics that drive fermentation. She develops predictive models that link microbial community composition to flavour outcomes, with the goal of making traditionally artisanal processes more reproducible without sacrificing their characteristic complexity. Her work integrates metabolomics profiling with real-time bioprocess monitoring.

equipment.name: Agilent 1260 HPLC System

people.name: Dr. Kwame Asante
people.bio: Kwame received his PhD in Mechanical Engineering from the University of Cape Town, where he designed haptic feedback systems for surgical robotics. He then worked at a robotics lab in Osaka focused on dexterous manipulation before joining the programme. He leads the SousBot project and co-leads the Sustainable Kitchen hardware initiative with Sofia.
people.researchDescription: Kwame's research centres on closed-loop sensory feedback systems for autonomous cooking. He designs robotic platforms that can sense temperature, texture, and aroma in real time and adjust cooking parameters accordingly. His current work on the SousBot integrates electronic nose sensors with robotic manipulation to create machines that can cook adaptively, responding to the actual state of the food rather than following fixed programmes.

people.name: Dr. Sofia Petridis
people.bio: Sofia completed her PhD in Environmental Science at the University of Amsterdam, studying life cycle assessment methods for agricultural systems. She previously worked as a sustainability consultant for a major European food retailer. Within the programme, she leads the Carbon Footprint of Deliciousness project and collaborates closely with Kwame on energy-efficient cooking hardware.
people.researchDescription: Sofia investigates the environmental trade-offs inherent in food production and preparation, asking whether deliciousness and sustainability can be optimised simultaneously. Her research applies multi-objective optimisation to map the Pareto frontiers between taste quality and carbon footprint across different ingredient sourcing strategies, cooking methods, and supply chain configurations.

people.name: Dr. Ravi Chandra
people.bio: Ravi earned his PhD in Plant Science from the John Innes Centre in Norwich, where he used CRISPR-Cas9 to modify terpene biosynthesis pathways in tomatoes. He spent a year at the Boyce Thompson Institute at Cornell before joining the programme. He leads the Genome to Gastronome project, working at the interface of crop genetics and flavour chemistry.
people.researchDescription: Ravi's research explores how genetic variation in crops translates into the flavour compounds we taste. He maps quantitative trait loci associated with flavour-relevant volatiles in heritage crop varieties and uses genome editing to enhance desirable flavour pathways. His long-term goal is to develop crop varieties that are simultaneously optimised for yield, nutrition, and taste.

equipment.name: Illumina MiSeq

people.name: Dr. Hannah O Brien
people.bio: Hannah completed her PhD in Nutritional Sciences at University College Dublin, investigating the relationship between gut microbiome composition and dietary preferences. She held a postdoctoral fellowship at the Nestlé Research Centre in Lausanne before joining the programme. She leads the Taste Matrix project on personalised flavour profiling.
people.researchDescription: Hannah's research focuses on understanding why individuals perceive and prefer different flavours, and how this knowledge can inform personalised dietary recommendations. She integrates nutrigenomic data, gut microbiome profiles, and metabolic modelling to predict individual responses to food. Her work on the Taste Matrix aims to create computational tools that can tailor flavour profiles to individual physiological and genetic characteristics.

equipment.description: Indirect calorimetry system for dietary intervention studies

people.name: Dr. Lukas Bergström
people.bio: Lukas received his PhD in Analytical Chemistry from Uppsala University, developing electronic nose arrays for clinical diagnostics. Before joining the programme, he worked at the Swedish National Food Agency on rapid pathogen detection methods. He leads the Sniff & Tell project on electronic nose networks for food spoilage detection.
people.researchDescription: Lukas works on sensor-based approaches to food safety, developing networks of electronic nose devices that can detect volatile organic compounds associated with spoilage and contamination. His research combines gas sensor array design with machine learning classification to create rapid, non-invasive methods for assessing food freshness and safety across supply chains.

people.name: Prof. Eleanor Whitfield
people.bio: Eleanor is Professor of Sensory Science at the University of Thornbridge, where she has led her research group for fifteen years. She trained as a chemist at Oxford before shifting to psychophysics during her PhD at Cambridge. She serves on the editorial board of Food Quality and Preference and has supervised over twenty doctoral students.
people.researchDescription: Eleanor's research group investigates the mechanisms by which chemical stimuli are translated into flavour perception. Her work spans the full chain from molecular interactions with taste and olfactory receptors through to cognitive integration and hedonic response. She has particular expertise in designing rigorous sensory panel methodologies and in the statistical analysis of perceptual data.

people.name: Prof. Kenji Yamamoto
people.bio: Kenji is Professor of Robotics and Food Engineering at the Lakemere Institute of Technology. He received his PhD from the University of Tokyo and spent a decade in industrial robotics at Fanuc before moving to academia. He has published over 150 papers on robotic manipulation and automated food processing.
people.researchDescription: Kenji's research focuses on the automation of complex food processing tasks that have traditionally resisted mechanisation due to the variability and delicacy of food materials. His group develops adaptive robotic systems that combine force sensing, computer vision, and compliant manipulation to handle foods ranging from fragile pastries to slippery noodles.

people.name: Prof. Amara Osei
people.bio: Amara is Professor of Fermentation Biochemistry at the University of Thornbridge. She completed her PhD at the University of Ghana and held a Royal Society Dorothy Hodgkin Fellowship before joining Thornbridge. Her research group has pioneered work on metabolic pathway analysis in mixed-culture fermentations.
people.researchDescription: Amara's research centres on the biochemistry of microbial communities in fermentation, with a particular focus on understanding how metabolic interactions between species give rise to the complex flavour profiles of traditionally fermented foods. Her group uses metabolic flux analysis, transcriptomics, and in situ spectroscopy to map the biochemical landscape of fermentations in real time.

people.name: Prof. David Chen
people.bio: David is Professor of Machine Learning at St. Aldhelm's University, where he leads the Applied AI Laboratory. He received his PhD from Stanford and worked at Google Research before returning to academia. He is a Fellow of the Alan Turing Institute and has received an ERC Consolidator Grant.
people.researchDescription: David's research group develops machine learning methods tailored to the specific challenges of scientific domains, including small datasets, noisy measurements, and the need for interpretable models. Within the programme, his team contributes expertise in predictive modelling, neural network architectures for structured chemical data, and statistical frameworks for complex experimental data.

people.name: Prof. Fiona McAllister
people.bio: Fiona is Professor of Agricultural Genomics at St. Aldhelm's University. She completed her PhD at the Roslin Institute in Edinburgh and spent five years at the International Rice Research Institute in the Philippines before joining St. Aldhelm's. She leads a large research group focused on crop improvement through genomics and gene editing.
people.researchDescription: Fiona's research uses genomic tools to understand and improve the flavour qualities of food crops. Her group combines genome-wide association studies, transcriptomics, and CRISPR-based editing to identify and modify the genetic pathways controlling flavour compound biosynthesis.

people.name: Prof. Raj Patel
people.bio: Raj is Professor of Analytical Chemistry at the Lakemere Institute of Technology, specialising in rapid detection methods for food contaminants. He received his PhD from Imperial College London and previously held a chair at the University of Nottingham. He serves as a scientific advisor to the Food Standards Agency.
people.researchDescription: Raj's research develops fast, sensitive, and field-deployable analytical methods for detecting pathogens, toxins, and adulterants in food. His group works on miniaturised sensor platforms, immunoassay technologies, and spectroscopic methods that can be deployed outside the laboratory.

people.name: Sam Thornton
people.bio: Sam is a second-year PhD student at the University of Thornbridge, supervised by Dr. Mei-Ling Zhao. He holds an MSc in Food Science from the University of Leeds, where his dissertation focused on the biochemistry of miso fermentation. His PhD investigates the molecular basis of umami perception in fermented foods.
people.researchDescription: Sam's research explores how fermentation processes generate umami-active compounds and how these interact with human taste receptors. He combines analytical chemistry — identifying and quantifying glutamates, nucleotides, and peptides in fermented products — with sensory panel data to build predictive models linking fermentation conditions to perceived umami intensity.

people.name: Aisha Bakari
people.bio: Aisha is a first-year PhD student at the Lakemere Institute of Technology, supervised by Dr. Kwame Asante. She graduated with distinction from the University of Lagos with a degree in Mechatronics Engineering. Her PhD focuses on developing robotic manipulation strategies for delicate culinary tasks.
people.researchDescription: Aisha's research tackles the challenge of programming robots to handle food with the dexterity and sensitivity of a human cook. She is developing adaptive gripping strategies that respond to the texture, temperature, and fragility of different ingredients, using a combination of tactile sensing, force control, and reinforcement learning.

people.name: Lucas Gomez
people.bio: Lucas is a second-year PhD student at St. Aldhelm's University, supervised by Dr. Tomás Eriksson. He has a background in computer science from the University of Buenos Aires and previously worked as a data engineer at a food delivery startup. His PhD develops machine learning approaches to recipe recommendation.
people.researchDescription: Lucas's research builds recommendation systems that go beyond simple ingredient matching to understand the deeper structure of culinary compatibility. He uses graph neural networks trained on the RecipeGraph knowledge base to suggest ingredient substitutions, novel pairings, and complete recipes tailored to user preferences, dietary constraints, and available ingredients.

people.name: Yasmin Al-Rashid
people.bio: Yasmin is a first-year PhD student at the University of Thornbridge, supervised by Dr. Mei-Ling Zhao. She holds an MSc in Microbiology from the University of Edinburgh, where she studied sourdough starter communities. Her PhD investigates the ecology of wild fermentation and its impact on flavour development.
people.researchDescription: Yasmin's research focuses on understanding the complex microbial communities that drive spontaneous fermentation — the wild yeasts and bacteria that produce the distinctive flavours of sourdough, natural wine, and traditional pickles. She uses metagenomic sequencing and metabolomic profiling to track how these communities assemble, compete, and cooperate.

equipment.name: BD Accuri C6 Plus Flow Cytometer
equipment.description: Cell counting and viability analysis for fermentation monitoring

people.name: James Wei
people.bio: James is a second-year PhD student at St. Aldhelm's University, supervised by Dr. Ravi Chandra. He completed his undergraduate degree in Genetics at the University of Hong Kong. His PhD uses functional genomics to understand flavour compound production in heritage crop varieties.
people.researchDescription: James's research investigates how genes controlling volatile compound biosynthesis are expressed differently across heritage and modern crop varieties. He uses RNA-seq, ATAC-seq, and reporter assays to map the regulatory landscape of flavour-associated genes in tomatoes and brassicas.

people.name: Nina Kowalski
people.bio: Nina is a first-year PhD student at the Lakemere Institute of Technology, supervised by Dr. Lukas Bergström. She has an MSc in Analytical Chemistry from the University of Warsaw. Her PhD develops improved methods for detecting volatile markers of food spoilage.
people.researchDescription: Nina's research focuses on identifying and characterising the volatile organic compound signatures associated with different types of food spoilage. She combines headspace gas chromatography-mass spectrometry with electronic nose sensor arrays to create comprehensive spoilage fingerprints.

people.name: Omar Hassan
people.bio: Omar is a second-year PhD student at St. Aldhelm's University, supervised by Prof. David Chen. He holds an MSc in Bioinformatics from King's College London. His PhD applies computational methods to understand microbial genomics in fermentation contexts.
people.researchDescription: Omar's research uses bioinformatic approaches to analyse the genomes and metagenomes of fermentation-associated microorganisms. He develops computational pipelines for assembling genomes from complex microbial communities and for predicting metabolic capabilities from genomic data.

people.name: Isla Thompson
people.bio: Isla is a first-year PhD student at the University of Thornbridge, supervised by Dr. Priya Ramanathan. She graduated from the University of Glasgow with a degree in Neuroscience. Her PhD investigates the neural basis of taste perception using computational modelling approaches.
people.researchDescription: Isla's research combines psychophysical experiments with computational neuroscience to model how the brain integrates taste, smell, and texture signals into a unified flavour experience. She uses EEG and behavioural data to test and refine mathematical models of multisensory integration.

people.name: Dev Patel
people.bio: Dev is a second-year PhD student at the Lakemere Institute of Technology, supervised by Dr. Kwame Asante. He has a BEng in Control Systems Engineering from the University of Mumbai and previously interned at a precision cooking startup. His PhD focuses on automation systems for sous-vide and other controlled cooking methods.
people.researchDescription: Dev's research develops intelligent control systems for precision cooking, with a focus on sous-vide techniques. He builds adaptive controllers that use real-time temperature and pressure data to optimise cooking profiles for different proteins and vegetables, accounting for variability in ingredient size, composition, and starting temperature.

people.name: Akiko Tanaka
people.bio: Akiko is a first-year PhD student at St. Aldhelm's University, supervised by Dr. Hannah O'Brien. She holds an MSc in Computational Biology from the University of Tokyo. Her PhD develops algorithmic approaches to personalised nutrition that account for individual genetic and microbiome variation.
people.researchDescription: Akiko's research builds computational models that predict how individuals will metabolise and respond to different foods based on their genetic profile and gut microbiome composition. She combines machine learning with physiological modelling to create personalised dietary recommendation algorithms.

people.name: Prof. James Liu
people.bio: James is Professor of Computational Science at the Lakemere Institute of Technology and Lead PI for Computational Methods within the programme. He received his PhD from MIT and has held visiting positions at INRIA and the Max Planck Institute for Intelligent Systems. He leads the programme's overall computational strategy.
people.researchDescription: James's research focuses on developing computational frameworks that can integrate heterogeneous data types — from genomic sequences to sensory panel scores — into unified predictive models. Within the programme, he ensures that the programme's diverse computational efforts are interoperable and that shared data infrastructure supports all projects.

people.name: Prof. Hannah Okonkwo
people.bio: Hannah is Professor of Biological Sciences at St. Aldhelm's University and Lead PI for Biological Sciences within the programme. She received her PhD from the University of Ibadan and was awarded a UKRI Future Leaders Fellowship early in her career. She oversees the programme's biological research strategy and coordinates postgraduate training.
people.researchDescription: Hannah's research background is in molecular biology and systems-level understanding of biological processes. Within the programme, she ensures that the programme's biological research — spanning fermentation, genomics, and nutrition — maintains scientific rigour and coherence. She leads the postgraduate training programme, designing a curriculum that equips PhD students with interdisciplinary skills.

Her expertise spans financial management, research governance, funder reporting, and stakeholder engagement. She works closely with the Lead PIs and institutional administrators to ensure the programme runs smoothly and that researchers can focus on their science.

projects.title: FlavorSpace: Topological Taste Perception Modelling
projects.description: Mathematical frameworks mapping taste perception as topological spaces, enabling novel flavour classification and prediction.
projects.abstract: The chemical space of flavour compounds is vast, high-dimensional, and poorly understood in terms of perceptual organisation. This project applies tools from topological data analysis—particularly persistent homology and mapper algorithms—to construct low-dimensional representations of flavour perception that respect the nonlinear structure of human taste. By integrating psychophysical data from trained sensory panels with molecular descriptor databases, we aim to build predictive models that map chemical structure to perceived flavour profiles. The resulting FlavorSpace framework will enable computational screening of novel ingredient combinations and inform rational flavour design.

slides.title: Research Question & Background
bullets: Taste perception is governed by ~400 olfactory receptors responding to thousands of volatile compounds in high-dimensional chemical space.
Current linear models (PCA, MDS) fail to capture nonlinear perceptual relationships that respect human sensory organization.
Central question: Can topological data analysis—persistent homology and mapper algorithms—reveal intrinsic structure in flavour perception enabling accurate prediction of novel compound profiles?

updates.author: Priya Ramanathan
updates.title: Cross-Cultural Flavour Topology: Preliminary Kyoto Collaboration Results
updates.content:
The Kyoto Taste Research Centre collaboration has yielded its first comparative dataset. We collected sensory panel data from 25 trained Japanese assessors using the same 200-compound panel tested by our UK cohort. The cross-cultural persistent homology analysis reveals that $H_0$ and $H_1$ features are remarkably stable across the two panels — the same 7 major taste clusters appear in both, with topological distances correlating at $\rho = 0.82$ (Spearman). However, $H_2$ features diverge significantly around the umami–savoury boundary, where Japanese panellists perceive finer-grained distinctions ($\beta_2 = 4$ persistent 2-cycles vs. $\beta_2 = 1$ in UK data).

The most striking result: wasabi-family isothiocyanates cluster within the 'pungent-fresh' region for Japanese assessors but fall in the 'irritant-bitter' region for UK assessors, with bottleneck distance between the two placements of $d_B = 0.41$ on persistence diagrams. This suggests the topological representation genuinely captures culturally-mediated perceptual organisation, not just chemosensory similarity.

We've begun applying the cross-cultural mapper graphs to identify 'universal' flavour relationships (stable across both panels) versus 'culturally contingent' ones. Preliminary count: ~68% of pairwise flavour affinities are universal, ~32% culturally contingent. The contingent relationships cluster heavily around fermented, bitter, and umami compounds — consistent with known dietary exposure effects on taste sensitivity.

Sam optimised the alpha-complex filtration and it now runs 40% faster than the sparse Rips approach on the expanded cross-cultural dataset (24,000 compounds × 2 panels). We're comfortably within interactive query times for the FlavorSpace visualisation tool. The methods paper draft for JCIM is nearly complete; targeting submission by mid-April.

updates.author: Priya Ramanathan
updates.title: March Progress Report: Dataset Expansion and Topology Refinement
updates.content:
Over the past quarter, we completed the second round of sensory panel trials with 45 participants, achieving our target sample size for the topological analysis. The persistent homology pipeline is now running reliably on the full molecular descriptor dataset (~12,000 compounds), though we encountered unexpected computational bottlenecks with the Vietoris-Rips complex at higher dimensions. We've adopted a sparse approximation method that reduces computation time by roughly 60% with minimal loss of topological features.

The key breakthrough this month was demonstrating that our topological descriptors outperform standard PCA-based dimensionality reduction for flavour compound clustering. On a held-out test set of 800 compounds, the persistent homology features achieved 84% classification accuracy for flavour family assignment, compared to 71% using PCA embeddings. This validates our core methodological bet and gives us a strong result for the upcoming methods paper.

We've also completed the integration of volatile organic compound (VOC) data from our upgraded GC-MS system. The higher-resolution molecular profiling has added approximately 3,000 new descriptor dimensions per compound. We were initially concerned about the curse of dimensionality, but the sparse Rips complex approach handles the expanded feature space well — computation time increased by only 25% despite the dimensionality increase.

On the collaboration front, we've begun weekly syncs with Hannah's personalised nutrition team to explore whether our flavour topology maps could inform dietary recommendation algorithms. Early results are promising — the embedding spaces show meaningful clusters that correlate with both sensory panel responses and nutritional profiles. We're exploring a joint paper that would bridge the two projects.

Sam has been invaluable in troubleshooting the computational pipeline and has proposed an alternative filtration approach using alpha complexes that could further reduce computation time. We plan to benchmark this against the current Rips approach over the next few weeks.

Next quarter priorities:
- Submit the methods paper to Journal of Chemical Information and Modeling (target: end of April)
- Present FlavorSpace interactive visualisations at the Spring Integration Workshop
- Begin integrating the cross-cultural flavour perception data from our collaboration with the Kyoto Taste Research Centre
- Recruit 15 additional sensory panelists for the extended validation study

updates.author: Priya Ramanathan
updates.title: December Update: Nature Food Acceptance
updates.content:
Excellent news: our manuscript "Topological Analysis of Taste Space: Novel Frameworks for Flavour Perception" has been accepted to Nature Food with minor revisions. The reviewers praised the mathematical rigor and the novel application of persistent homology to sensory science. We've incorporated reviewer feedback and submitted the revision.

The main revision request was to include a more extensive comparison with standard chemoinformatic approaches (molecular fingerprints, MACCS keys, etc.). We added a supplementary analysis showing that our topological features capture non-linear perceptual relationships that fingerprint-based methods miss entirely — particularly for compounds that are structurally dissimilar but perceptually similar (e.g. certain esters and aldehydes that share fruity notes).

We also completed calibration of our sensory panel protocols, achieving inter-rater reliability of 0.91 on descriptor consistency. This high agreement gives us confidence in the underlying sensory data feeding the topology algorithms. The panel now includes 30 trained assessors, which exceeds the ISO 8586 recommendation for analytical sensory studies.

Hardware-wise, we upgraded the GC-MS system in the chemistry lab, which will allow us to profile volatile organic compounds at higher resolution. This should significantly improve our molecular descriptor accuracy. The upgrade cost was shared with the SousBot team, who will use the same equipment for their olfactory sensor calibration work.

Finally, we've received an invitation to present at the Gordon Research Conference on the Science of Food next summer, which would be an excellent venue for our topological framework. We plan to present the full FlavorSpace interactive tool there.

updates.author: Priya Ramanathan
updates.title: September Milestone: Proof-of-Concept Complete
updates.content:
We have successfully completed the topological proof-of-concept using persistent homology on a 150-compound dataset. The Mapper algorithm generated a 3D simplicial complex with clear clusters corresponding to known flavour families (fruity, floral, woody, etc.), validating our core hypothesis.

The sensory panel ratings showed strong concordance with topological proximity — compounds close in the topological space were rated as similar in flavour by panelists. Specifically, the Spearman correlation between topological distance and sensory dissimilarity ratings was 0.78 (p < 0.001), which is substantially higher than correlations achieved using standard molecular similarity metrics (Tanimoto coefficient: 0.52).

We ran the analysis on three separate sensory panel cohorts to test robustness, and the topological structure was remarkably consistent across groups — the same major clusters appeared in all three, with only minor variations in boundary compounds. This reproducibility is encouraging and suggests the topological representation captures genuine perceptual organisation rather than panel-specific biases.

We've documented all methods in an internal technical report (TR-FS-001) and begun writing the first manuscript. We also recruited two additional panelists to expand the sensory cohort to 25 participants for the next phase. Sam is working on optimising the computational pipeline to handle the target dataset of 12,000 compounds, which will require moving from a brute-force Rips complex to an approximate approach.

feedback.author: Prof. Eleanor Whitfield
feedback.title: Comments on March Progress
feedback.content:
Excellent progress on the topological descriptors vs PCA comparison — the 84% vs 71% result is the kind of clean, quantitative evidence we need for the methods paper. A few thoughts:

- The collaboration with Hannah's nutrition team is exactly the kind of cross-programme connection we hoped for. I'd encourage you to formalise this as a joint deliverable rather than keeping it informal — it strengthens both projects' impact narratives.
- On the GC-MS integration: make sure we're documenting the instrument parameters and calibration protocols thoroughly. If other groups want to replicate our molecular profiling approach, they'll need this.
- For the Spring Workshop presentation, consider including a live demo of the interactive FlavorSpace visualisation rather than static slides. It would make a much stronger impression.

Overall very pleased with the trajectory. The Nature Food acceptance was a major milestone and the follow-up work is building nicely on that foundation.

feedback.author: Prof. James Liu
feedback.title: Thoughts on Nature Food revision and next steps
feedback.content:
Congratulations on the Nature Food acceptance — well-deserved. The reviewer's request for comparison with chemoinformatic approaches was predictable but your response was thorough.

Two suggestions looking ahead:

- The cross-cultural flavour perception angle (Kyoto collaboration) could be a differentiator for the programme as a whole, not just this project. Consider presenting this at an operations committee meeting so we can think about whether other projects could contribute data or methods.
- I'd like to see a clear roadmap for making the FlavorSpace tool accessible to non-specialists. The topology mathematics is powerful but if only our group can use it, the impact is limited. A simplified API or web interface should be on the roadmap for next year.

currentChallenges.description: Sensory panel members reporting wildly inconsistent results on umami compounds. Three panellists now insist MSG tastes purple.

responses.author: priya
responses.content: Investigated the three panellists — turns out they all attended the same FlavorSpace demo last month where we showed colour-coded topology visualisations. Their 'purple' responses correlate exactly with the colour assigned to the umami cluster in our mapper graph. This is a priming effect rather than genuine synaesthesia. Retraining session scheduled with recalibrated references and no visual aids. In the meantime we're excluding their umami ratings from the current analysis; the remaining 42 panellists show normal inter-rater reliability (ICC = 0.89) on umami descriptors.

resolvedChallenges.description: Vietoris-Rips complex computation hitting memory limits (>128 GB) at dimension 3 on the full 12,000-compound dataset, blocking higher-dimensional homology analysis.
resolvedChallenges.resolutionNote: Migrated from brute-force Vietoris-Rips to a sparse alpha-complex filtration using the GUDHI library. Memory footprint dropped from 128 GB to ~18 GB, computation time reduced by 60%. The approximation preserves all persistent features with lifetime > 0.05 (verified against exact computation on a 2,000-compound subset). Now running H₀–H₃ on the full dataset in under 4 hours on a single GPU node.

projects.title: RecipeGraph: Knowledge Graphs for Culinary Reasoning
projects.description: Building semantic knowledge graphs of recipes, ingredients, and techniques to enable AI-driven recipe innovation.
projects.abstract: Culinary reasoning requires understanding complex relationships between ingredients, cooking techniques, cultural contexts, and desired outcomes. This project constructs a comprehensive semantic knowledge graph representing recipes, ingredients, cooking methods, and their interconnections. By leveraging linked data principles and ontological frameworks, we enable machine learning systems to perform recipe generation, ingredient substitution, and technique adaptation at scale. The system learns implicit culinary rules and flavor harmonies from over 500,000 recipes and can generate novel recipes that satisfy user constraints while maintaining culinary coherence.

updates.author: Tomas Eriksson
updates.title: Cultural Cuisine Evolution Analysis and Embedding Space Geography
updates.content:
The cultural cuisine evolution analysis is producing genuinely novel findings. By projecting our 500k-recipe knowledge graph into a 128-dimensional TransE embedding space and then clustering by cuisine metadata, we can trace historical flavour exchange between culinary traditions.

Key results from the embedding geography:

| Cuisine pair | Cosine similarity | Historical exchange |
|---|---|---|
| Portuguese–Japanese | 0.71 | Tempura, castella cake (16th c.) |
| Moorish–Spanish | 0.68 | Almonds, saffron, citrus (8th–15th c.) |
| French–Vietnamese | 0.64 | Bánh mì, pâté, café (19th–20th c.) |
| British–Indian | 0.62 | Kedgeree, curry powder, chutneys |
| Chinese–Peruvian | 0.58 | Chifa cuisine, soy-aji amarillo fusion |

These embedding distances correlate strongly with documented historical contact periods ($\rho = 0.74$, Spearman, $n = 42$ cuisine pairs with known exchange history). Notably, the embedding captures the *directionality* of influence: Portuguese→Japanese edges cluster around frying techniques and egg-rich confections, while Japanese→Portuguese edges are nearly absent, reflecting the asymmetric historical exchange.

We also identified 'bridge ingredients' — nodes with high betweenness centrality that connect otherwise distant cuisine clusters. Coconut milk, garlic, chilli, and lime emerge as the top four, which aligns with their documented role as pantry staples across tropical cuisines. The fifth, interestingly, is fish sauce — its graph centrality is driven by its appearance in Southeast Asian, Roman (garum), and Scandinavian (surströmming-adjacent) traditions.

On the LLM integration front: David and I prototyped a thin GPT-4o wrapper that translates natural language queries ('what could I make with leftover lamb and some pomegranate?') into SPARQL graph queries. Early results are promising — the wrapper correctly routes 78% of test queries to the appropriate subgraph, and the graph-grounded answers are substantially more culinarily coherent than direct LLM generation.

updates.author: Tomas Eriksson
updates.title: March Update: IUI Presentation and User Feedback
updates.content:
We successfully presented RecipeGraph at ACM IUI 2026 in late March to excellent reception. The venue had a large audience of HCI and AI researchers, and we received several collaboration inquiries from food tech companies. The abstract has been published online and we're preparing a full paper submission for the journal track.

We've also been analyzing user interactions from the beta API (launched Jan 2026). Over 2,500 users have registered, with 18,000+ unique recipe generation requests. User satisfaction scores are high (4.2/5), with particular praise for ingredient substitution accuracy and the ability to handle dietary constraints. The most common use case is allergy-aware recipe modification (38% of requests), followed by cuisine fusion suggestions (22%) and nutritional optimisation (18%).

An interesting finding from the usage data: users frequently chain multiple recipe modifications — starting with one substitution, then requesting another based on the result. This sequential reasoning pattern suggests our graph architecture is well-suited to iterative cooking exploration, which is a behaviour we hadn't anticipated in the original design.

We're currently working on a follow-up paper analyzing the implicit culinary knowledge encoded in our graph — how the embedding spaces reveal cultural cuisine clusters and historical flavour evolution. The preliminary results show clear geographic clustering in the embedding space, with interesting outliers where cuisine traditions have historically exchanged techniques (e.g. Portuguese-Japanese fusion evident in tempura-related nodes).

The most common use case is allergy-aware recipe modification (38% of requests), followed by cuisine fusion suggestions (22%) and nutritional optimisation (18%).

An interesting finding from the usage data: users frequently chain multiple recipe modifications — starting with one substitution, then requesting another based on the result. This sequential reasoning pattern suggests our graph architecture is well-suited to iterative cooking exploration, which is a behaviour we hadn't anticipated in the original design.

We're currently working on a follow-up paper analyzing the implicit culinary knowledge encoded in our graph — how the embedding spaces reveal cultural cuisine clusters and historical flavour evolution. The preliminary results show clear geographic clustering in the embedding space, with interesting outliers where cuisine traditions have historically exchanged techniques (e.g. Portuguese-Japanese fusion evident in tempura-related nodes).

updates.author: Tomas Eriksson
updates.title: November: Knowledge Graph Complete at 500k Recipes
updates.content:
We reached a major milestone: integration of 500,000 recipes from multiple sources (AllRecipes, Food.com, traditional cuisine databases from 12 countries). The complete graph now spans 50,000 unique ingredients and 1,200+ cooking techniques, making it one of the largest structured culinary knowledge bases in existence.

Our embedding models (trained on recipe similarity and ingredient co-occurrence) now capture nuanced flavour affinities. We validated the embeddings against expert chef judgments of ingredient pairing appropriateness — our model achieves 87% agreement with expert pairs, up from 75% at the 100k recipe stage. The improvement plateaued around 400k recipes, suggesting diminishing returns from additional recipe data alone.

We also completed the culinary ontology, formalizing relationships like 'is_variant_of', 'complements_with', 'substitutable_for', and 'technique_for'. This structured knowledge is proving invaluable for constraint-based recipe generation. Lucas contributed an elegant inference engine that can derive implicit relationships — for example, inferring that if A substitutes for B and B complements C, then A may also complement C (with appropriate confidence weighting).

We ran a small user study (n=15, mix of professional chefs and home cooks) to evaluate recipe generation quality. Participants rated our generated recipes higher than GPT-4 generated recipes on culinary coherence (4.1 vs 3.6 on 5-point scale) and ingredient compatibility (4.3 vs 3.4). However, GPT-4 scored higher on creativity (3.8 vs 3.2), suggesting our knowledge graph approach is more conservative. We're investigating how to increase creative suggestions while maintaining culinary soundness.

updates.author: Tomas Eriksson
updates.title: August Progress: Core Architecture and First 100k Recipes
updates.content:
We've completed the core RecipeGraph architecture using RDF (Resource Description Framework) and OWL (Web Ontology Language). The system can now ingest structured recipe data and automatically infer new relationships through ontology reasoning.

We integrated the first 100,000 recipes from a major public dataset. Early graph embeddings (using TransE algorithm) are showing promise — ingredient substitution suggestions now match expert intuition ~75% of the time. We experimented with several embedding approaches (TransE, RotatE, ComplEx) and found TransE performs best for substitution tasks while RotatE captures hierarchical ingredient relationships more accurately.

The data pipeline now handles automated extraction from semi-structured recipe websites. We built a custom NER (Named Entity Recognition) model for ingredient parsing that handles quantities, preparation methods, and brand names with 93% F1 score. This was a significant engineering effort but is essential for scaling beyond curated datasets.

We presented preliminary results at the international Knowledge Graphs for Food symposium and received positive feedback. Three domain experts from leading culinary schools have agreed to advise the project, which will be invaluable for validating our ontology design decisions.

feedback.title: CropToPlate perspective on recipe-side integration
feedback.content: From the CropToPlate side, the cold-start behaviour is the interesting bit here. If RecipeGraph can surface plausible early recipe matches for unfamiliar cultivars, that would make the genomics-to-recipe handoff much easier to explain to non-technical collaborators.

Prof. David Chen
feedback.title: Thoughts on IUI results and LLM integration
feedback.content:
Great presentation at IUI — I heard very positive feedback from the programme committee. The usage data from the beta API is particularly valuable; the sequential modification pattern you identified is a genuine research contribution in itself.

On the LLM integration idea: I think this is worth pursuing but we need to be careful about scope. Suggest framing it as a thin interface layer over the existing graph rather than a fundamental architectural change. The graph's structured reasoning is our differentiator — the LLM should translate natural language to graph queries, not replace the graph with generative approaches.

Also worth connecting with Priya's FlavorSpace work. Your ingredient embeddings and her topological flavour maps are representing similar information from different angles. A joint analysis could be very compelling.

feedback.title: Impressive demo at IUI
feedback.content: Saw the IUI demo write-up and had a chance to play with the substitution API. responses.author: tomas

projects.title: The Fermentation Whisperer: Predictive Microbial Modelling
projects.description: Machine learning models predicting microbial fermentation outcomes and flavour development from process conditions.
projects.abstract: Fermentation is a complex bioprocess where microbial communities produce flavour compounds and preserve food through metabolic activity. This project develops machine learning models that predict fermentation outcomes—including microbial dynamics, flavour compound production, and shelf-life—from initial conditions, substrate composition, and process parameters. By integrating metabolomics data with microbial sequencing and fermentation kinetics, we create predictive frameworks that enable rational optimization of fermentation processes. These models will accelerate product development and enable real-time process monitoring in industrial settings.

updates.author: Mei-Ling Zhao
updates.title: Community Succession Modelling: Predictive Power of Early-Stage ASV Dynamics
updates.content:
## Motivation

Our prediction pipeline has relied on process parameters (temperature, pH, salt, substrate) as input features. The missing piece has been **direct microbial community composition** at early timepoints — specifically, whether amplicon sequence variant (ASV) abundances at day 2 carry enough signal to predict fermentation outcomes at day 14+.

This update reports results from a systematic study across 180 fermentation runs (tempeh $n=60$, kimchi $n=55$, kombucha $n=40$, kvass $n=25$).

## Methods

We extracted 16S rRNA amplicon data at $t = \{0, 2, 5, 7, 14\}$ days for each batch. Community composition was summarised as relative abundances of the top 200 ASVs. We fitted three model families:

- **Gradient boosting (XGBoost)** on day-2 ASV abundances alone
- **LSTM recurrent network** on the full $(t_0, t_2, t_5)$ trajectory
- **Hybrid model**: XGBoost on concatenated process parameters + day-2 ASVs

Target variable: final acidity ($\Delta\text{pH}$ from inoculation to day 14), binned into three classes (mild, moderate, sharp) for classification metrics, and continuous for regression.

## Key Results

### Classification accuracy (3-class acidity prediction)

| Model | Accuracy | Macro-F1 | AUC-ROC |
|---|---|---|---|
| Process parameters only (baseline) | 0.78 | 0.74 | 0.86 |
| Day-2 ASVs only | 0.83 | 0.81 | 0.91 |
| LSTM on $(t_0, t_2, t_5)$ | 0.81 | 0.78 | 0.89 |
| Hybrid (process + day-2 ASVs) | **0.91** | **0.89** | **0.96** |

The hybrid model substantially outperforms all single-source models. The LSTM, despite having access to more temporal data, underperforms XGBoost on day-2 snapshots — consistent with our earlier finding that microbial succession in these matrices follows relatively deterministic kinetics.

### Keystone ASV analysis

SHAP feature importance identifies **8 keystone ASVs** whose day-2 abundance accounts for $>65\%$ of the model's predictive variance:

1. *Lactobacillus plantarum* (ASV-003) — strongest single predictor across all matrices
2. *Leuconostoc mesenteroides* (ASV-011) — early dominance predicts milder final acidity
3. *Pediococcus pentosaceus* (ASV-027) — interaction with salt concentration is key
4. *Acetobacter pasteurianus* (ASV-041) — critical in kombucha; negligible in kimchi

The remaining four are matrix-specific and less individually informative.

### Regression on continuous $\Delta\text{pH}$

The hybrid model achieves $R^2 = 0.87$ (MAE $= 0.12$ pH units) on held-out test data. Residual analysis shows the largest errors occur in wild-fermented kvass, where uncharacterised environmental microbiota introduce stochastic variation. Restricting to controlled-inoculation batches gives $R^2 = 0.93$.

## Succession dynamics

We fitted generalised Lotka–Volterra (gLV) models to the time-series data:

$$\frac{dx_i}{dt} = x_i \left( r_i + \sum_{j=1}^{N} a_{ij} x_j \right)$$

where $x_i$ is the relative abundance of ASV $i$, $r_i$ is the intrinsic growth rate, and $a_{ij}$ captures pairwise interactions. Fitting via regularised least squares ($\ell_1$ penalty, $\lambda = 0.01$) recovers a sparse interaction network dominated by **competitive exclusion** between *L. plantarum* and *L. mesenteroides*, with *P. pentosaceus* acting as a facilitator species in high-salt environments.

The gLV model's 7-day-ahead predictions of community composition achieve a Jensen–Shannon divergence of $0.08 \pm 0.03$ from observed distributions — a meaningful improvement over the naive persistence baseline ($\text{JSD} = 0.19 \pm 0.07$).

## Implications for the monitoring dashboard

We have integrated the hybrid model into Yasmin's real-time monitoring system. When a new batch reaches day 2 and 16S results are available (turnaround ~6 hours with our MinION protocol), the dashboard now displays a predicted acidity trajectory with 90% confidence intervals. In the last two weeks, this caught a kombucha batch trending toward excessive vinegar character — the brewer adjusted temperature down by 2°C and the batch recovered to target profile.

## Next steps

- Validate the gLV interaction network against **co-culture knockout experiments** (removing individual species and measuring community response)
- Test whether the day-2 prediction model generalises to the sake brewery data (different matrix, different dominant organisms)
- Investigate whether **metabolomic features** at day 2 (VOC profiles from the e-nose) can substitute for 16S in settings where sequencing turnaround is too slow

updates.author: Mei-Ling Zhao
updates.title: March Update: Industrial Partnerships Begin
updates.content:
This has been a pivotal month for the project's translational ambitions. We've formalised three industrial pilot studies with mid-size fermentation producers (tempeh, kimchi, and sake producers). Each manufacturer will use our predictive models to optimise their fermentation processes in parallel with traditional methods for a 6-month comparison period.

The sake brewery partnership is particularly interesting from a scientific perspective. They run 30-40 batches per season across 8 sake grades, each with detailed koji cultivation logs going back 15 years. This historical data is a goldmine — we can validate our models against known outcomes and potentially identify optimisation opportunities the brewers haven't spotted. The challenge is data format integration; their records are a mix of handwritten logs (now digitised) and modern sensor data, so Yasmin is building a custom ETL pipeline to harmonise everything.

We also finalised the core machine learning pipeline, achieving >92% accuracy on microbial community prediction. The gradient boosting ensemble outperforms LSTM models on this dataset, likely because microbial succession follows relatively deterministic kinetics rather than complex temporal dependencies. We ran a thorough ablation study showing that initial inoculum composition and temperature profile account for ~65% of prediction variance. Interestingly, the time-of-year variable has a small but statistically significant effect (p=0.03), probably via ambient humidity affecting water activity.

Yasmin has built an impressive real-time monitoring dashboard for the lab fermentation vessels. The system ingests IoT sensor data every 30 minutes, runs predictions, and flags batches deviating from expected trajectories. We trialled this over the past two weeks and caught one tempeh batch heading toward off-flavour development — the early warning allowed us to intervene (temperature adjustment) and rescue the batch.

Our Trends in Food Science & Technology paper was accepted and is in proof stage. We've also submitted preliminary results on metabolomic flavour signatures to Food Chemistry for an upcoming special issue on fermentation biotechnology.

Next quarter priorities:
- Onboard the sake brewery historical data (15 years of logs)
- Deploy monitoring dashboard at tempeh producer's facility as a field test
- Investigate whether 16S rRNA integration can improve wild fermentation prediction
- Present the real-time monitoring approach at the Spring Workshop

updates.title: November Milestone: >90% Prediction Accuracy
updates.content:
Excellent progress: we achieved >90% accuracy on predicting microbial community composition at day 7 of fermentation. The random forest model trained on 150 experiments generalises well to held-out test fermentation batches (20 additional experiments). This is a milestone we've been working toward since the project started, and hitting it with a comfortable margin gives us confidence in the approach.

We identified 15 metabolite biomarkers that reliably predict sensory quality (sourness, umami intensity, fruity notes). These metabolites correlate strongly with both microbial species presence and fermentation parameters, suggesting they capture the mechanistic relationship between process and flavour. The most informative biomarkers are diacetyl (buttery notes), acetic acid (vinegar sharpness), and a cluster of branched-chain aldehydes associated with malty/roasty character.

We also completed data collection from 50 spontaneous vegetable fermentations, expanding our dataset to include uncontrolled starter cultures. Early models suggest we can predict wild fermentation success rates even without known inoculum, though accuracy drops to ~70% compared to ~92% for controlled inoculation. The key missing variable appears to be the initial microbial load and diversity of the raw vegetables, which varies enormously between suppliers and seasons.

We've started conversations with the Good Bug, Bad Bug team about sharing microbial sequencing protocols. Their 16S rRNA pipeline could complement our sensor-based approach by providing direct information about microbial community composition at key timepoints during fermentation.

updates.author: Mei-Ling Zhao
updates.title: August Update: Dataset Ready, Baseline Models Built
updates.content:
We completed data collection from 120 controlled fermentation experiments across 4 food types (tempeh, kimchi, kombucha, kvass). Each experiment includes 16S microbial sequencing (resolution to genus level), GC-MS metabolomics (200+ volatile compounds), and 30+ process parameters (temperature, pH, salt, substrate composition).

We built baseline machine learning models (decision trees, random forests, gradient boosting) predicting microbial composition from process parameters. Initial results show ~75% accuracy, with temperature and salt concentration being the strongest predictors. We experimented with several feature engineering approaches and found that interaction terms between temperature and salt concentration improve predictions by about 3%, which makes biological sense since salt tolerance is temperature-dependent for many lactic acid bacteria.

Yasmin has developed an automated data collection pipeline using IoT sensors in our fermentation lab. The system uses Raspberry Pi-based sensor nodes with pH probes, thermocouples, and dissolved oxygen sensors, feeding into an InfluxDB time-series database. The total hardware cost per fermentation vessel is approximately £150, which is very reasonable for the data quality we're getting.

We also established collaborations with two industrial partners interested in applying these models to optimise fermentation reproducibility and quality control.

feedback.title: Student note on modelling handoff and lab usability
feedback.content: From the student side, the industrial partnership work is exciting, but the current data handoff still assumes a fairly expert user. A short note on what a production lab technician actually needs to see from the model would make the translational story stronger and easier to defend in committee discussion.

Prof. Amara Osei
feedback.title: Feedback on industrial partnerships and translational strategy
feedback.content:
The industrial partnerships are a great development and I'm pleased to see the project moving toward real-world validation. A few points:

- Make sure the data sharing agreements are properly formalised through the university's technology transfer office before you start receiving production data. Happy to help facilitate this — I have contacts in the TTO from previous collaborations.
- The real-time monitoring dashboard Yasmin built sounds impressive. I'd like to see a demo at the next group meeting. We should also think about whether this could become a standalone tool that other labs could deploy.
- The sake brewery's 15-year historical dataset is a unique resource. Consider whether there's a standalone data paper opportunity there — the descriptive statistics and trends alone would be valuable to the fermentation science community.

feedback.title: Cross-project note on gLV modelling and genomic integration
feedback.content:
Mei — read through the community succession update with interest. A few observations from the genomics side:

The gLV interaction coefficients you're recovering look plausible, but I'd urge caution about interpreting them mechanistically without validation. Regularised least-squares on compositional data can produce spurious interactions — the $\ell_1$ penalty helps with sparsity but doesn't address the simplex constraint on relative abundances. Have you looked at SPIEC-EASI or SparCC as alternatives? They handle compositionality more rigorously and might change the topology of your interaction network, particularly the facilitator role you're attributing to *P. pentosaceus*.

On the 16S side: genus-level resolution may be masking important strain-level variation. In the NutriGenome Atlas project we've seen cases where two strains of the same species have opposite metabolic phenotypes — one producing diacetyl, the other consuming it. If your predictive accuracy plateaus, shotgun metagenomics or even long-read 16S (we have the MinION protocol optimised for full-length V1–V9) could unlock the next increment.

The sake brewery dataset is exciting. Worth flagging: traditional koji cultivation involves *Aspergillus oryzae* strains that are heavily domesticated. The interaction dynamics in a fungal-bacterial mixed community will look very different from your current lactic-acid-bacteria-dominated systems. Your gLV model may need a separate parameterisation for fungal fermentations rather than a single unified model.

Happy to lend sequencing capacity if you want to run a pilot with deeper resolution on a subset of your 180 batches. We have spare flow cells this quarter.

feedback.author: Prof. Amara Osei
feedback.title: Feedback on industrial partnerships and translational strategy
feedback.content:
The industrial partnerships are a great development and I'm pleased to see the project moving toward real-world validation. A few points:

- Make sure the data sharing agreements are properly formalised through the university's technology transfer office before you start receiving production data. Happy to help facilitate this — I have contacts in the TTO from previous collaborations.
- The real-time monitoring dashboard Yasmin built sounds impressive. I'd like to see a demo at the next group meeting. We should also think about whether this could become a standalone tool that other labs could deploy.
- The sake brewery's 15-year historical dataset is a unique resource. Consider whether there's a standalone data paper opportunity there — the descriptive statistics and trends alone would be valuable to the fermentation science community.

feedback.title: Good Bug, Bad Bug integration question
feedback.content: Looking at the industrial trial planning — does the contamination detection step include real-time sequencing, or is it still relying on the e-nose + metabolite panel? Our diagnostic protocol could plug in cleanly if there's an API surface. Happy to set up a call with Lukas and Mei if useful.

projects.abstract: Consistent culinary outcomes require continuous monitoring and adjustment of cooking parameters based on sensory feedback. This project develops a robotic cooking system that integrates multiple sensory modalities—thermal, optical, and olfactory—into closed-loop control systems. The system uses electronic nose technology, thermographic imaging, and machine vision to continuously assess food state and adjust heating, stirring, and other parameters in real-time. By implementing feedback control algorithms and learning from expert demonstrations, SousBot achieves consistent sensory outcomes across multiple executions, enabling reliable automation of complex cooking techniques.

updates.author: Kwame Asante
updates.title: Closed-Loop Thermal Regulation: Benchmark Results
updates.content:
## Summary

The SousBot platform now achieves closed-loop temperature regulation with a mean absolute error of $\pm 1.0\,°\text{C}$ from target across three standardised cooking tasks — a **70% improvement** over the open-loop baseline ($|e| = 3.3\,°\text{C}$). A lightweight surface-state classifier (MobileNet-v3-Small, deployed on the Jetson Orin Nano) reaches **92.9% mean accuracy** across six cooking-surface states (raw, sweat, brown, caramel, char, burn), with per-class performance ranging from 88.6% (caramel) to 97.2% (raw).

The sensing stack consists of a FLIR Lepton 3.5 thermal camera ($160 \times 120\,\text{px}$), an 8-channel MOx e-nose array, and an RGB-D stereo camera, all feeding frames at $\sim$2 ms intervals into the classifier.

## Control Model

The induction actuator output $u(t)$ is governed by a discrete PID law:

$$u[k] = K_p \, e[k] + K_i \, T_s \sum_{j=0}^{k} e[j] + \frac{K_d}{T_s}(e[k] - e[k-1])$$

where $e[k] = T_{\text{target}} - \hat{T}[k]$ is the error signal $s(t)$ from the classifier, and $T_s = 42\,\text{ms}$. Gains were tuned via Ziegler–Nichols on the caramelisation task ($K_p = 2.4$, $K_i = 0.8$, $K_d = 0.3$). The control signal $u(t)$ drives both the induction actuator and a 3-DOF stirring arm.

## Benchmark Results

| Task | $T_{\text{target}}$ (°C) | MAE open-loop (°C) | MAE closed-loop (°C) | Reduction |
|---|---|---|---|---|
| Caramelisation | 180 | 3.8 | 1.2 | 68% |
| Emulsion maintenance | 72 | 2.9 | 0.8 | 72% |
| Starch gelatinisation | 96 | 3.1 | 1.1 | 65% |
| **Mean** | | **3.3** | **1.0** | **70%** |

The open-loop baseline exhibits sustained oscillation (panel a of the benchmark figure), while the closed-loop PID controller converges within approximately 25 seconds on all tasks (panel b). The caramel–char boundary remains the hardest surface-state classification transition ($\Delta\varepsilon < 0.02$ in the 8–14 μm band), with caramel state accuracy at 88.6% being the lowest of the six classes.

### Per-class surface-state accuracy

| State | Accuracy (%) |
|---|---|
| Raw | 97.2 |
| Sweat | 93.1 |
| Brown | 91.8 |
| Caramel | 88.6 |
| Char | 90.4 |
| Burn | 96.1 |

## Steam Occlusion Problem

High-moisture tasks produce a vapour column between cooking surface and the FLIR sensor (see §4 of the architecture diagram). We model the observed radiance as:

$$L_{\text{obs}}(\lambda) = \tau(\lambda, d) \cdot L_{\text{surface}}(\lambda) + [1 - \tau(\lambda, d)] \cdot L_{\text{vapour}}(\lambda, T_w)$$

where $\tau(\lambda, d) = e^{-\alpha(\lambda) d}$ is the transmittance of the vapour column of depth $d$. At $d > 8\,\text{cm}$, classifier accuracy drops below 80%. Two mitigation paths under investigation: polarimetric filtering and a learned correction term $\hat{\tau}(d)$ from a secondary humidity sensor.

## Next Steps

- Quantify polarimetric filter performance across $d \in [5, 15]\,\text{cm}$
- Extend benchmarks to dynamic-temperature tasks (staged searing: 230°C → 160°C step reduction)
- Submit steam-interference findings to *IEEE Sensors Journal* (target: May 2026)

updates.author: Kwame Asante
updates.title: March Update: v2 Prototype with NLP Integration
updates.content:
We successfully integrated the NLP interface (developed in collaboration with Tomas's SousBot Speaks project) into the hardware prototype. The system can now parse natural language cooking instructions ("sear the beef until golden brown", "cook until soft and creamy") and translate them into sensory feedback control targets. This is a significant step toward making robotic cooking accessible to non-technical users.

Testing on simple techniques (egg cooking, sauce reduction) shows 87% success rate. The system occasionally struggles with ambiguous instructions — "cook until done" for example has no clear sensory target, so the system falls back to conservative time-temperature defaults. Active learning from user corrections is improving the models; after 50 correction cycles, the ambiguous instruction success rate has improved from 62% to 74%.

We've also optimised the electronic nose calibration, improving volatile compound recognition from 24 to 32 distinct compounds. The new compounds include several Maillard reaction intermediates that help the system distinguish between "browning" and "burning" — a critical distinction for closed-loop control. Aisha contributed a novel sensor array configuration that improved discrimination between chemically similar volatiles by 15%.

Hardware-wise, we added a mechanical arm for stirring (3 DOF, food-safe stainless steel, torque-limited for safety) and are testing a new thermal camera with improved thermal resolution (±0.3°C, up from ±0.5°C). The new camera also supports higher frame rates (120Hz vs 50Hz), which is important for monitoring rapid state changes like oil reaching smoke point.

We ran a systematic evaluation comparing SousBot-cooked meals against professional chef-cooked meals in a blinded sensory panel (n=24). Results: SousBot achieved comparable scores on consistency (4.1 vs 4.3/5) but lower scores on presentation (3.2 vs 4.5/5) and creative adaptation (2.8 vs 4.7/5). This confirms our system's strength in precision and consistency while highlighting that aesthetic and creative aspects remain firmly in the human domain.

Next major milestone: closing the loop on a complex technique (roux preparation — requires simultaneous temperature control, stirring rate adjustment, and colour monitoring) by end of Q2. This would be a compelling demo for the programme's annual review.

One note for programme context: the commercial partnership conversation has slowed slightly because the potential pilot kitchen wants a clearer view of installation constraints and food-safety sign-off for the v2 rig. This is not a technical blocker, but it does mean the partnership milestone now depends on a better operational handoff than we first expected.

updates.author: Kwame Asante
updates.title: November: Sensor Calibration Complete, Paper Accepted
updates.content:
Excellent news: our IEEE RA-L paper "SousBot: Autonomous Cooking with Sensory Feedback Control" was accepted after minor revisions. The reviewers particularly praised the integrated sensory approach and control algorithms.

We completed full sensor calibration across the three sensing modalities. The thermal camera achieves ±0.5°C accuracy across 20-250°C range. The e-nose achieves 95%+ classification accuracy on 15 distinct cooking-relevant volatiles (caramel, maillard products, burnt notes, etc.). Machine vision segmentation for food state achieves 92% IoU on held-out test images.

We conducted 30 closed-loop cooking trials (steaks, chicken, vegetables) and achieved 91% consistency on color-based doneness endpoints. This is a major validation that sensory feedback can overcome cooking variability.

updates.author: Kwame Asante
updates.title: September: Hardware Prototype Complete
updates.content:
We successfully completed the hardware prototype (v1) assembly and initial testing. The system integrates:
- Thermal imaging camera (320x256 resolution, 50Hz sampling)
- Electronic nose (SAW sensors, 32-channel VOC detection)
- Stereo RGB-D camera for food state imaging
- Motor control for heating element and stirring arm
- Embedded Linux computer running the control algorithms

Initial open-loop tests on steak searing show baseline variability of ~40% in browning consistency (comparing across 5 identical trials). We've implemented basic feedback control (adjust heat based on food surface temperature), reducing variability to 18%.

Next phase: integrate the electronic nose signals into the feedback controller and test on more complex techniques.

feedback.author: Prof. Kenji Yamamoto
feedback.title: Comments on v2 prototype and blinded evaluation
feedback.content:
The blinded sensory evaluation results are very interesting and I think they tell a nuanced story. The comparable consistency scores (4.1 vs 4.3) are the headline result — this validates the core engineering approach. The lower presentation and creativity scores are expected and, frankly, not the problem we're trying to solve.

For the roux demonstration, I'd suggest documenting not just the final quality but the failure modes — what happens when the system encounters unexpected input (wrong flour type, butter at wrong temperature). Understanding failure gracefully is what distinguishes a robust system from a demo.

The NLP integration with SousBot Speaks is looking promising. I notice the success rate drops for ambiguous instructions — this is worth studying in its own right. What makes a cooking instruction unambiguous? There might be a nice HCI paper there.

feedback.author: Prof. Eleanor Whitfield
feedback.title: Feedback on IEEE RA-L acceptance and next steps
feedback.content:
Congratulations on the IEEE RA-L acceptance — that's a strong venue and well-deserved. The integrated sensory approach is the project's key differentiator and the reviewers clearly recognised that.

Two thoughts for the next phase:
- The e-nose calibration improvement (24 to 32 compounds) is technically impressive but I'd like to understand the practical impact better. Which of the new compounds actually improve cooking outcomes? Not all detectable volatiles are actionable.
- Consider whether the blinded evaluation methodology could be standardised and offered to other groups in the programme. Several projects could benefit from rigorous sensory evaluation protocols.

feedback.author: Aisha Bakari
feedback.title: Comments on thermal regulation benchmarks and steam occlusion
feedback.content:
The benchmark results are solid — the 70% MAE reduction is a clear validation of the closed-loop approach. Two observations from the sensor side:

The steam occlusion model is useful but the transmittance decay you're seeing at 8 cm is probably worse in practice than in bench tests. In real cooking the vapour column isn't static — convection currents create turbulent mixing that causes rapid SNR fluctuations. I'd suggest logging frame-by-frame SNR variance alongside the mean, because a classifier that works at SNR 0.6 steady-state might fail at 0.6 with high variance.

On the polarimetric filtering path: I ran some preliminary tests with wire-grid polarisers on the Fermentation Whisperer's thermal array (similar FLIR module) and found that the polarisation contrast between surface emission and scattered vapour is measurable but small — around 3–5% difference in degree of linear polarisation. That might not be enough for robust filtering. The humidity sensor correction path might be more practical. Happy to share the polarisation data if useful.

The MobileNet-v3 accuracy at the browning–caramelisation boundary (88.6%) could probably improve with a temporal model — single-frame classification throws away the trajectory information. A simple sliding-window approach over 5–10 frames might help the classifier use the rate of spectral change, not just the instantaneous state.

projects.description: Optimising food production for both taste quality and environmental sustainability using multi-objective algorithms.
projects.abstract: Food production must balance organoleptic quality, nutritional value, and environmental impact. This project develops multi-objective optimization frameworks that simultaneously maximize sensory quality and minimize environmental footprint across the food supply chain. By integrating life cycle assessment data with sensory science models and taste prediction systems, we identify Pareto-optimal ingredient combinations and production methods. The framework enables food companies to reformulate products for sustainability while maintaining consumer-perceived quality and flavor profiles.

updates.author: Sofia Petridis
updates.title: March Update: Food Company Partnerships and Expansion
updates.content:
We've initiated partnerships with 5 major food manufacturers to test our optimization framework on real product formulations. The first pilot involves a tomato sauce producer—our model identified a reformulation using 40% heritage tomato blend that reduces carbon footprint by 32% while maintaining sensory scores above 4.2/5 (threshold for consumer acceptability).

We expanded our case study to include peppers and cucumbers. The multi-objective landscape is more complex for peppers (10+ sensory attributes), but preliminary Pareto frontiers are emerging. We've also begun incorporating water scarcity indices into the optimization, particularly relevant for Mediterranean crops.

Our EST paper is now in press, and we're invited to present at the American Chemical Society meeting in April. Response to the framework from industry contacts has been very positive.

updates.author: Sofia Petridis
updates.title: November: EST Paper Published, Case Study Complete
updates.content:
Our paper "Carbon-Optimised Food Production: Balancing Taste and Sustainability" was published in Environmental Science & Technology. The paper presents the complete multi-objective optimization framework with a detailed tomato case study.

Key findings: Using heritage tomato varieties combined with optimized irrigation and integrated pest management, we can reduce carbon footprint by 35% compared to conventional production while improving sensory quality. The Pareto frontier reveals meaningful trade-offs—for instance, 10% additional carbon reduction possible by switching to older cultivars with slightly lower yield.

We also completed life cycle assessment (LCA) data collection for 50+ tomato varieties from diverse agro-climatic regions. This dataset is now public and will be valuable for other researchers.

updates.author: Sofia Petridis
updates.title: August: Sustainability Metrics Framework Defined
updates.content:
We completed the sustainability metrics framework, integrating carbon footprint, water use, land use, and biodiversity indices. The framework standardizes LCA calculations across different production methods and scales.

We also compiled comprehensive sensory data: 200+ consumer sensory panels rating 40 tomato varieties on sweetness, acidity, umami, texture, and overall appeal. Consumer preferences vary regionally—European panelists prefer higher acidity; US panelists prefer higher sweetness.

We implemented the first multi-objective optimization algorithm (NSGA-II) and tested it on a simplified tomato production scenario. The Pareto frontier is beginning to reveal trade-offs: organic methods have lower carbon but higher land requirements.

currentChallenges.description: Carbon footprint calculator returns negative values for the vegan lasagne recipe. Mathematically interesting but nutritionally suspicious.

feedback.author: Prof. Amara Osei
feedback.title: Thoughts on the food manufacturer partnerships and scope expansion
feedback.content:
The 5 manufacturer partnerships are a great development. One concern: expanding to peppers and cucumbers before the tomato case study is fully validated risks spreading the team too thin. The tomato Pareto frontiers are your strongest result — I'd suggest making those watertight (including the regional consumer preference variation) before broadening.

On the water scarcity integration: this is the right direction, and you should look at what the Sustainable Kitchen project is doing with their energy-efficiency lifecycle models. There may be a shared methodological framework for multi-dimensional sustainability scoring that would strengthen both projects.

For the ACS presentation in April, lead with the 32% carbon reduction at maintained acceptability result. That's the number that will resonate with industry attendees. The Pareto methodology is interesting to academics but the headline needs to be the practical outcome.

projects.title: From Genome to Gastronome: Flavour Pathway Engineering
projects.description: Enhancing flavour compounds in heritage crops through targeted genetic engineering and phenotypic selection.
projects.abstract: Many heritage crop varieties possess superior flavour profiles but poor agronomic traits, limiting their commercial cultivation. This project applies genomic selection and CRISPR-based engineering to enhance flavour pathway expression in crops while maintaining agronomic performance. Through quantitative trait locus mapping, candidate gene identification, and precision editing, we enhance expression of key volatile organic compounds and taste-active molecules. The project focuses on heritage varieties of tomatoes, peppers, and cucurbits, creating crops that deliver superior sensory experiences without sacrificing yield or disease resistance.

Central question: Can metabolic flux modeling + machine learning on transcriptomic data predict flavor outcomes of targeted gene knockouts and overexpression in heritage crop varieties?
