updates.author: Ravi Chandra
updates.title: Flux Balance Modelling Predicts Volatile Outcomes of Double Knockouts
updates.content:
Following Fiona's recommendation, we adapted the NutriGenome Atlas metabolic model for *Solanum lycopersicum* and ran flux balance analysis (FBA) on the terpenoid biosynthesis pathway before proceeding with the next round of CRISPR edits.

The FBA predictions for our existing single-knockout lines match observed GC-MS volatile profiles with $R^2 = 0.87$ ($n = 6$ lines, 15 volatiles each). The model correctly predicted the unexpected geraniol accumulation in the TPS21 knockout — the flux redistribution through the GPP pool was evident in the constraint-based simulation. This gives us confidence to use FBA as a pre-screening tool for planned combinatorial edits.

We simulated 45 double-knockout combinations targeting terpene synthases and cytochrome P450 enzymes. The model predicts 8 combinations that should enhance fruity ester production (ethyl butanoate, ethyl hexanoate) by >2× without depleting the monoterpene pool that contributes floral notes. Three of these are now in the CRISPR pipeline; we expect T0 transformants within 6 weeks.

Separately, the pepper QTL fine-mapping is complete. We narrowed the three terpene-controlling regions to intervals of 1.2 Mb, 0.8 Mb, and 2.1 Mb respectively. Candidate gene analysis identified 7 terpene synthases and 3 transcription factors within these intervals. RNA-seq on contrasting accessions (high-terpene vs. low-terpene) shows differential expression for 4 of the 7 TPS genes ($\log_2 \text{FC} > 2$, FDR < 0.01).

The Molecular Plant revision was accepted — publication expected in the May issue.

updates.author: Ravi Chandra
updates.title: March Update: CRISPR Lines Performing Well in Field Trials
updates.content:
We're pleased with the progress of our 6 CRISPR-edited tomato lines in field trials (planted November 2025). All lines show the expected enhanced expression of fruity volatile esters (particularly ethyl esters), with 2.5-3.0× increase over wild-type controls.

Agronomic performance is excellent: yield is 95-98% of wild-type, disease resistance (to early blight and late blight) is maintained or improved, and fruit quality metrics (color, firmness, sugar content) are comparable.

We also completed QTL fine-mapping on pepper accessions. We identified 3 genomic regions controlling terpene expression (important for peppery and fruity notes). Plan to create CRISPR-edited pepper lines by Q3.

Our Molecular Plant paper is in revision with reviewers; we expect acceptance in Q2.

updates.author: Ravi Chandra
updates.title: October: Heritage Crop Panel Sequencing Complete
updates.content:
Excellent milestone: we completed whole-genome sequencing of 120 heritage tomato and 80 heritage pepper accessions from our breeding program. The diversity is remarkable—accessions span multiple continents and show substantial genetic variation in flavor-related genes.

We performed detailed phenotyping on 200 plants from diverse accessions: measuring 15 volatile organic compounds (via GC-MS), sugar content, acidity, and 10+ taste-active molecules. Sensory panels (50+ trained panelists) rated all varieties on 10 sensory attributes.

We began QTL analysis on the combined genomic and phenotypic dataset. Early results show strong association between terpene synthase polymorphisms and perceived "spicy" or "fruity" notes in peppers and tomatoes respectively.

updates.author: Ravi Chandra
updates.title: July: Project Kickoff and Germplasm Assembly
updates.content:
We officially kicked off the Genome to Gastronome project with a team assembly meeting. The core team includes plant biologists, food scientists, and bioinformaticians.

We assembled a heritage crop germplasm collection: 120 heirloom tomato varieties and 80 pepper landraces from diverse geographical origins. Many varieties are known for exceptional flavor but are rarely cultivated due to poor agronomic traits.

We established protocols for standardized sensory evaluation (trained panel) and chemical analysis (GC-MS, HPLC). We also set up the molecular breeding laboratory, including access to CRISPR-Cas9 equipment and plant transformation facilities.

currentChallenges.description: Ethics board wants to know if teaching an AI to dislike cilantro constitutes programming bias. Review pending.

responses.author: ravi
responses.content: I've drafted a response for the ethics board. Our position: the OR6A2 genetic variant genuinely affects perception of cilantro aldehyde compounds, so the model is encoding a documented biological relationship, not a bias. Sent to Sofia for review before submission.

resolvedChallenges.description: Plant transformation efficiency for heritage pepper accessions extremely low (<2% T0 recovery), blocking the CRISPR editing programme for peppers.
resolvedChallenges.resolutionNote: Optimised the Agrobacterium-mediated transformation protocol: switched to strain AGL1, increased acetosyringone concentration to 200 µM during co-cultivation, and extended shoot regeneration phase from 4 to 6 weeks on modified MS media with 2 mg/L BAP. T0 recovery rate now 8–12% across 5 tested accessions, sufficient for our experimental needs. Protocol documented and shared with the wider team.

feedback.author: Prof. Fiona McAllister
feedback.title: Flavour pathway validation and CRISPR strategy
feedback.content:
Ravi — the GWAS results on volatile QTLs are solid but I want to flag a risk with the CRISPR flavour pathway engineering. Editing single pathway genes in isolation can have unexpected effects on connected metabolic networks. The limonene synthase you're targeting also feeds into the monoterpene branch that produces linalool and geraniol — knocking it up could deplete precursors for other flavour compounds.

I'd recommend running a flux balance analysis on the terpenoid pathway before making the next round of edits. The NutriGenome Atlas team has a metabolic model for Solanum lycopersicum that could be adapted. Happy to connect you with Hannah if you haven't already discussed this.

The CropToPlate integration is working well from what I can see — making sure your engineered lines flow into Tomas's recommendation pipeline is exactly the kind of cross-project synergy the programme needs.

projects.title: You Are What You Digest: Personalised Nutrition Models
projects.description: Computational models predicting individual responses to foods based on genetics, microbiome, and metabolism.
projects.abstract: Nutritional science is shifting toward personalized approaches that account for individual genetic variation, microbiome composition, and metabolic phenotypes. This project develops predictive models of how individual consumers will respond metabolically and sensorially to different foods and nutrient profiles. By integrating genomic data, microbiome sequencing, metabolomic profiles, and longitudinal sensory preference records, we create person-specific nutritional models. These enable food companies and nutritionists to provide genuinely personalized dietary recommendations and enable the design of foods targeted to individual metabolic and sensory needs.

updates.author: Hannah O Brien
updates.title: Clinical Trial Protocol Approved; Microbiome-Satiety Mechanism Identified
updates.content:
Two significant developments this month.

First, the 200-person randomised clinical trial received ethics approval from the Aldhelm University IRB (protocol AUIRB-2026-0147). The trial design is a 12-week parallel-group study comparing personalised multi-omic dietary recommendations against standard UK Eatwell Guide advice. Primary endpoint: change in HbA1c and fasting glucose at 12 weeks. Secondary endpoints include diet adherence (food diary + app tracking), self-reported satiety, and microbiome composition shift. Recruitment opens next week; we're targeting 50% of participants from outside the university to address Eleanor's representativeness concern.

Second, and more scientifically exciting: we identified a candidate mechanism for the *Faecalibacterium prausnitzii*–satiety association. Metagenomic analysis of the short-chain fatty acid (SCFA) pathway reveals that high-*F. prausnitzii* individuals produce significantly more butyrate ($\text{mean} = 14.2 \pm 3.1 \text{ mmol/kg}$ vs. $8.7 \pm 2.8$ in low-abundance individuals, $p < 0.001$). Butyrate is a known GLP-1 secretagogue, and our CGM + appetite hormone data show that high-butyrate producers have 28% higher postprandial GLP-1 peaks. This provides a mechanistic chain: *F. prausnitzii* → butyrate → GLP-1 → prolonged satiety.

We're now testing whether prebiotic supplementation (inulin, 12 g/day) can shift microbiome composition toward higher *F. prausnitzii* abundance in a 4-week pilot within our existing cohort. If successful, this could become an actionable dietary recommendation within the personalised nutrition framework.

The pilot app now has 95 active users. We've added a meal photo recognition feature (using a fine-tuned ResNet50 on the nutrient database) that estimates macronutrient composition from food images with 79% accuracy.

updates.author: Hannah O Brien
updates.title: March Update: Nutrients Paper Published, Pilot App Launch
updates.content:
Excellent news: our paper "Personalised Nutrition Algorithms: From Genetics to Plate" was published in Nutrients. The paper presents the complete multi-omic framework and demonstrates 84% accuracy in predicting individual responses to 50 test meals.

We also launched the pilot app (web-based) for personalized nutrition recommendations. Early users (60 participants) report 89% satisfaction with recommended meals. The app takes DNA results, microbiome profile, and sensory preferences as input and generates personalized dietary recommendations with predicted satisfaction and health benefit scores.

Next major step: initiate a 200-person clinical trial to measure whether personalized recommendations improve long-term diet adherence and health outcomes (vs. standard dietary guidelines).

updates.author: Hannah O Brien
updates.title: November: Dataset Complete, Model Performance at 84%
updates.content:
Major milestone: completed multi-omic data collection from 150 participants. Each participant provided:
- Whole-genome sequencing (30× coverage)
- 16S microbiome profiling (stool samples)
- Metabolomics (plasma untargeted and targeted)
- Sensory preference data (50 test meals, 15 taste attributes each)
- 6-month dietary recall and health biomarkers

We trained integrated machine learning models predicting taste preferences and metabolic responses. Accuracy reached 84% on held-out test meals. Random forests and gradient boosting performed equally well; microbiome composition was the strongest single predictor (76% accuracy), but multi-omic integration critical for reaching 84%.

We also identified specific microbial taxa and genetic variants associated with strong taste preferences (e.g., Bacteroides vulgatus associated with salt preference; TAS1R2 variants associated with sweet preference).

updates.author: Hannah O Brien
updates.title: August: Genetic Algorithm Framework Established
updates.content:
We completed the core genetic algorithm framework for optimizing personalized nutritional recommendations. The framework uses machine learning to predict individual health outcomes and taste preferences, then optimization algorithms search the space of possible diets for personalized recommendations.

We enrolled 150 participants in the study; 50 have completed baseline testing (genome sequencing, microbiome sampling, metabolomics). We also compiled a comprehensive nutrient database (500+ foods with detailed macronutrient, micronutrient, and bioactive compound profiles).

Early machine learning models (trained on 50 participants) show promising correlations between microbiome composition and taste preferences, validating our hypothesis that the microbiome influences sensory perception.

currentChallenges.description: CRISPR tomato line 7 has developed unexpected resistance to being photographed. All spectrophotometry readings normal but camera images consistently blurry. Possibly cursed.

responses.author: hannah
responses.content: Not cursed — the enhanced trichome density on line 7 fruit creates a fine surface haze that scatters light at close range. The macro lens autofocus hunts on the fuzzy surface. Manual focus at f/8 or higher produces sharp images. Ravi's spectrophotometer doesn't care because it integrates over a large spot size. Mystery solved, but the trichome phenotype is interesting in its own right — may affect volatile release kinetics.

resolvedChallenges.description: CGM (continuous glucose monitor) data from 30 participants showing implausible negative glucose excursions, corrupting the postprandial response dataset.
resolvedChallenges.resolutionNote: Traced to a firmware bug in the Libre 3 sensors from a specific production batch (lot #L3-2025-09). The sensor occasionally returns raw ADC values instead of calibrated glucose readings during rapid temperature changes (e.g., entering/leaving cold rooms). Replaced all affected sensors and applied a post-hoc correction to salvageable data using the manufacturer's calibration curve. 22 of 30 affected participants' data recovered; 8 required repeat testing.

feedback.author: Prof. Eleanor Whitfield
feedback.title: Participant recruitment and cross-project data sharing
feedback.content:
The 150-participant cohort is a good start but I'm concerned about demographic representativeness. The university recruitment pool skews young (18–30), educated, and UK-resident. The microbiome-taste-preference correlations you're finding may not generalise to older adults or different dietary traditions.

For the next recruitment round, can we partner with the NHS Biobank cohort? They have existing microbiome and dietary data on a much more representative population. I have a contact in the Biobank governance team who could advise on access.

Also: the genetic algorithm framework for personalised nutrition is closely related to what Priya is doing in the Taste Matrix project with flavour-preference modelling. Have you compared notes on your respective taste-preference prediction models? There may be opportunities to share training data and avoid duplicating the sensory panel work.

projects.description: Distributed electronic nose sensor networks for real-time detection of food spoilage and quality degradation.
projects.abstract: Food spoilage remains a major source of waste throughout supply chains. This project develops distributed networks of electronic nose sensors that detect volatile organic compounds associated with microbial spoilage and enzymatic degradation. By training machine learning models on comprehensive volatile fingerprints of spoiling foods, we create systems that can predict remaining shelf-life with high accuracy. The network architecture enables real-time monitoring of food quality in storage facilities and during transport, providing early warning of spoilage before it becomes organoleptically apparent.

updates.author: Lukas Bergström
updates.title: Fermented Food Volatilomics: Expanding the E-Nose Beyond Fresh Produce
updates.content:
We've started the planned extension to fermented and processed foods, and the volatilomics landscape is significantly more complex than fresh produce.

We collected 8-week time-series e-nose profiles from 4 fermented food matrices: kimchi, tempeh, natural yoghurt, and sourdough. Each matrix was monitored at 6-hour intervals across its typical fermentation and storage lifecycle. The dataset now includes 1,200 new volatile fingerprints.

The core challenge: fermented foods produce many of the same volatile organic compounds (ethanol, acetic acid, diacetyl, dimethyl sulphide) during *normal* fermentation that our existing models associate with spoilage in fresh foods. Naively applying the fresh-produce classifier to fermented foods yields a 62% false positive rate — the system thinks everything is spoiled.

Our solution is a two-stage classification architecture:

1. **Matrix identifier** (random forest, 97% accuracy on 12-class food type): determines whether the sample is a fresh or fermented product
2. **Matrix-specific spoilage model**: applies the appropriate VOC baseline and deviation thresholds

For kimchi specifically, we identified 3 VOC signatures that discriminate normal acidification from genuine spoilage (*Clostridium* contamination): butyric acid spike >0.8 ppm, 1-propanol:ethanol ratio >0.3, and trimethylamine presence. These achieve 89% sensitivity / 93% specificity on held-out kimchi samples ($n = 80$).

Kenji's suggestion about MEMS sensors is well taken. We're running a parallel comparison: our current SAW array vs. a Sensirion SGP41 MEMS VOC sensor (£4.50 per unit). Preliminary data suggests the MEMS sensor captures 70% of the discriminative information at 1/60th the cost — potentially good enough for retail deployment of the binary fresh/spoiled classifier, with the full SAW array reserved for detailed spoilage typing.

updates.author: Lukas Bergström
updates.title: March Update: Shelf-Life Prediction Models Validated
updates.content:
Excellent progress on shelf-life prediction models. We completed validation on 200 held-out test samples spanning 8 food types (apples, lettuce, tomatoes, milk, yogurt, fish, chicken, bread). Models achieved:
- Produce: 94% accuracy predicting shelf-life within ±1 day
- Dairy: 88% accuracy within ±1 day
- Meat/Fish: 91% accuracy within ±12 hours

We also developed a quantitative shelf-life score (0-100) that retailers can use for dynamic pricing and inventory management. Early feedback from retail partners is very positive—they see potential to reduce waste and optimize promotions.

Our Food Control paper was published and received substantial media attention, generating interest from supply chain companies.

updates.author: Lukas Bergström
updates.title: November: E-Nose Sensor Prototype Complete and Calibrated
updates.content:
We completed assembly and calibration of the electronic nose sensor prototype. The system uses 32-channel SAW (Surface Acoustic Wave) sensors optimized for food spoilage volatiles. Calibration involved 60+ reference compounds and showed excellent linear response (R² > 0.99) across detection range (ppb to ppm).

We began systematic spoilage experiments: controlled decay of 15 different foods (lettuce, apples, yogurt, milk, fish, chicken, bread, etc.) under standard conditions. We collected volatile profiles at 6-hour intervals until organoleptically spoiled. Dataset now includes 300 time-series profiles (~5,000 unique volatile fingerprints).

We trained initial machine learning models (random forests) for spoilage classification. Early results show 87% accuracy distinguishing fresh from spoiled samples; shelf-life prediction models in progress.

updates.author: Lukas Bergström
updates.title: August: Sensor Network Architecture and Protocol Design
updates.content:
We established the technical architecture for the E-Nose sensor network. Design includes:
- Individual sensor nodes (SAW sensor array + embedded Linux + Bluetooth)
- Edge processing (local ML models for real-time classification)
- Cloud backend for model updates and cross-facility learning
- Mobile/web interfaces for facility managers and retailers

We also defined data collection and validation protocols. We're partnering with 3 produce wholesalers and 2 dairy processors to source real spoilage data in natural conditions.

First prototype sensor assembled and tested; showed promising volatile detection capabilities. Next phase: systematic spoilage experiments to train machine learning models.

currentChallenges.description: Electronic nose prototype v3 cannot distinguish between truffle oil and a PhD student who has been in the lab for 36 hours. Calibration urgently needed.

responses.author: lukas
responses.content: Identified the root cause: both truffle oil (2,4-dithiapentane) and human body odour after extended lab sessions share overlapping thioether signatures in the SnO₂ sensor channels. Added a WO₃ channel specifically tuned to the 350°C operating point where 2,4-dithiapentane has a distinct response curve from the shorter-chain thioethers in sweat. Cross-validated on 40 blind samples — discrimination accuracy now 96%. Also installed an air filtration unit in the lab as a secondary measure.

resolvedChallenges.description: Sensor drift over 72+ hour continuous monitoring sessions causing false spoilage alerts on day 3+ of long-duration meat storage experiments.
resolvedChallenges.resolutionNote: Implemented automated baseline recalibration every 6 hours using a sealed reference headspace (clean air + 3 reference VOCs at known concentrations). The recalibration cycle takes 90 seconds and corrects for both thermal drift and sensor poisoning. Validated over a 14-day continuous monitoring trial on chicken samples — no false alerts after day 3. Drift correction algorithm published as supplementary material in the Food Control paper.

feedback.author: Prof. Kenji Yamamoto
feedback.title: Hardware integration and deployment path
feedback.content:
The 93% shelf-life prediction accuracy is impressive. From an engineering perspective, a few thoughts on the deployment path:

The current sensor node prototype (SAW array + embedded Linux + Bluetooth) is fine for lab validation but the BOM cost (~£280 per node) will be prohibitive for widespread retail deployment. For the commercial version, have you looked at MEMS-based metal oxide sensors? They're less sensitive but 10× cheaper and could be good enough for the binary fresh/spoiled classification even if they can't do the full spoilage-type discrimination.

The edge processing architecture is well designed. One suggestion: add a confidence score to the real-time classification output. Facility managers need to know when the sensor is uncertain (e.g., due to ambient VOC interference) rather than getting a false-confident 'spoiled' call that causes them to discard good product.

We should also discuss integration with SousBot's sensory pipeline — the e-nose sensor data format is compatible and there may be shared calibration protocols.

updates.author: Priya Ramanathan & Hannah O Brien
updates.title: March Joint Report: Taste Matrix System Integrated
updates.content:
Major milestone: we successfully integrated the FlavorSpace topology models with the TasteTrix multi-omic predictions to create the first version of the Taste Matrix system. The integrated system takes an individual's sensory profile (FlavorSpace coordinates) and genetic/microbiome/metabolic data (TasteTrix features) and jointly optimizes to recommend foods that maximize both flavor satisfaction AND nutritional benefit.

We completed validation on 100 pilot participants. Taste Matrix recommendations achieved 88% mean predicted satisfaction (measured by sensory models) vs. 62% for standard dietary guidelines. Actual participant feedback confirmed high satisfaction with recommendations (4.3/5 rating).

We've also initiated a clinical trial with 200 participants to measure real-world health outcomes (weight, blood lipids, inflammation markers) over 6 months. Early retention rates are excellent (95% after 1 month).

updates.author: Priya Ramanathan & Hannah O Brien
updates.title: December: Model Integration Planning Complete
updates.content:
We completed the technical planning for integrating FlavorSpace and TasteTrix models. The integration strategy involves:

1. Feature alignment: mapping TasteTrix multi-omic features to FlavorSpace taste coordinates
2. Joint optimization: developing algorithms that simultaneously optimize flavor satisfaction (via topology) and nutritional metrics (via genomic/microbiome predictions)
3. Recommendation system: building a searchable food database scored on both flavor and nutritional personalization

We also created preliminary mock-ups of the Taste Matrix app and conducted focus groups with 20 participants. Initial feedback very positive: people find the idea of personalized flavor+nutrition compelling.

updates.author: Priya Ramanathan & Hannah O Brien
updates.title: October: Cross-Project Alignment Meeting
updates.content:
We held the kickoff meeting for the Taste Matrix collaboration. Both FlavorSpace and TasteTrix teams aligned on the technical approach and timeline.

Key insight: FlavorSpace's topological maps of taste preference + TasteTrix's genomic/microbiome predictions are highly complementary. FlavorSpace captures perceptual structure; TasteTrix captures metabolic determinants of satisfaction. Integrating both should enable powerful personalization.

We've started building shared datasets: 50 participants now have both topological taste profiles (FlavorSpace sensory panels) and comprehensive multi-omic profiles (TasteTrix genomic/microbiome). Next phase: train joint models on this data.

currentChallenges.description: Pilot participants keep asking why their personalised flavour profile insists they are "58% broth-forward". Explainability layer needs work before wider rollout.
Microbiome feature import pipeline is drifting from the sensory topology schema after every weekly refresh, which means recommendation scores wobble more than they should.

responses.author: tomas
responses.content: The schema drift is coming from my side — RecipeGraph's weekly vocabulary update changes the embedding dimension order. I'll pin the export schema to a versioned snapshot so Priya's import pipeline has a stable target. Fix should be in by Friday.

feedback.author: Prof. Amara Osei
feedback.title: Sensory panel methodology and the microbiome integration
feedback.content:
The personalised flavour profiling work is coming together nicely. A few methodological points:

The 200-participant sensory panel is producing good data but I notice you're using a 9-point hedonic scale for preference. The food science literature has been moving toward labelled affective magnitude (LAM) scales — they give better discrimination at the extremes and avoid the ceiling effects you're seeing with the 9-point scale on familiar foods. Worth considering for the next round of panelling.

The microbiome → taste preference link is the most novel part of this work. The correlation you've found between Prevotella abundance and bitter sensitivity is consistent with recent literature on gut-brain axis signalling. But correlation isn't causation — do you have a plan for a causal test? A dietary intervention study (shifting microbiome composition via prebiotic supplementation) with pre/post taste sensitivity measurement would be very compelling, even with a small cohort (n=20–30).

projects.description: Connecting agricultural genomics outputs directly to recipe systems for optimal ingredient utilisation.
projects.abstract: Advances in crop genomics enable production of new crop varieties with novel trait combinations, yet these varieties are often underutilized due to unfamiliarity. By characterizing the chemical and sensory profiles of new varieties and mapping these to recipe knowledge graphs, the system identifies optimal culinary applications and generates novel recipes that showcase unique variety characteristics, accelerating adoption of improved crop varieties.

updates.author: Tomas Eriksson & Ravi Chandra
updates.title: March Proof-of-Concept Demo Complete
updates.content:
We successfully completed the proof-of-concept demo for CropToPlate. The system took 5 newly bred heritage tomato varieties (from Genome to Gastronome breeding program) and automatically:

1. Characterized their flavor/texture profiles (via GC-MS and sensory evaluation)
2. Mapped these profiles into RecipeGraph ingredient space
3. Generated 80+ novel recipes showcasing unique variety characteristics
4. Ranked recipes by "fit" (how well variety traits are utilized) and "novelty" (how different from existing recipes)

We presented results to 8 expert chefs who reviewed the generated recipes. 85% rated the recommendations as "promising" or "innovative". Several chefs were particularly interested in using newly characterized varieties in their restaurants.

We filed a patent application covering the automated variety-to-recipe pipeline.

updates.author: Tomas Eriksson & Ravi Chandra
updates.title: December: Integration Architecture Complete
updates.content:
We completed the technical architecture for CropToPlate. The system integrates:

1. Genome to Gastronome outputs: new crop variety genotypes and phenotypes
2. Chemical/sensory profiling pipeline: standardized measurement of flavor/texture attributes
3. RecipeGraph ingredient embedding space: mapping varieties to recipe knowledge graph coordinates
4. Recipe recommendation engine: identifying optimal recipes for each variety

We established data sharing agreements between projects and created a shared database of 20 varieties with complete genomic, phenotypic, and culinary characterization.

We also surveyed 50+ chefs and food professionals about their needs for new variety information; strong interest in culinary recommendations as complement to agronomic data.

updates.author: Tomas Eriksson & Ravi Chandra
updates.title: September: Collaborative Project Kickoff
updates.content:
We held the kickoff meeting for CropToPlate, bringing together RecipeGraph and Genome to Gastronome teams. Key insight: new crop varieties with improved agronomic traits often have unique flavor profiles that chefs aren't familiar with—culinary recommendations could significantly accelerate adoption.

We identified a first set of 10-15 promising varieties (from the Genome to Gastronome breeding program) for characterization and recipe mapping. We established the collaboration workflow and began building the shared data infrastructure.

Recipe recommender keeps matching high-acidity breeding lines to desserts because it has discovered pavlova and refuses to let go.

responses.author: priya
responses.content: This is a flavour-space embedding issue. The acidity dimension in our embedding collapses dessert acids (citric, tartaric) with savoury acids (acetic, lactic). If we split the acidity axis into sugar-context and salt-context sub-dimensions, the recommender should stop conflating salsa verde tomatoes with meringue toppings.

resolvedChallenges.resolutionNote: Service engineer replaced the ion source filament and recalibrated. Backlog of 8 lines processed in a 4-day intensive run. Preventive maintenance schedule now quarterly instead of biannual.

feedback.author: Prof. David Chen
feedback.title: Patent strategy and the chef evaluation methodology
feedback.content:
Two points on the proof-of-concept demo:

The patent application for the variety-to-recipe pipeline is important but the claims need tightening. As filed, the independent claim covers 'automated mapping of crop genotype to culinary application via knowledge graph embedding' — this is broad enough that prior art from flavour-pairing databases (Ahn et al. 2011, FlavorDB) could be cited against it. I'd recommend narrowing to the specific genomic-prediction-to-recipe-graph pipeline, which is genuinely novel.

On the chef evaluation: 85% of chefs rating recommendations as 'promising or innovative' is a good headline, but the methodology could be stronger. Were the chefs blind to whether they were evaluating AI-generated vs. human-curated recommendations? If not, novelty bias (rating AI output higher out of curiosity) could inflate the score. A proper blind evaluation with a human-curated control arm would make the eventual paper much stronger.

projects.abstract: Fermentation safety requires rapid, accurate distinction between beneficial fermentation microbes and pathogenic contamination. This project develops integrated diagnostic platforms combining electronic nose technology with metabolomic analysis and rapid DNA sequencing to identify microbial communities in real-time. Machine learning models trained on comprehensive microbial signatures enable detection of spoilage-associated and pathogenic organisms within hours rather than days. The system provides early warning of fermentation failure and contamination, enabling intervention before product loss occurs.

slides.title: Research Question & Background
bullets: Fermentation outcomes depend critically on microbial species composition; spoilage organisms (Clostridium, Acetobacter, molds) produce off-flavors while beneficial LAB (Lactobacillus, Pediococcus) produce preferred flavor.

Current fermentation practice uses undefined culture mixtures or environmental selection; rapid strain identification (16S rRNA alone cannot distinguish species-level variation in flavor production capacity).

Central question: Can whole-genome sequencing + metabolic phenotyping of fermentation isolates enable rapid identification of flavor-positive vs. flavor-negative strains, and guide starter culture design?

bullets: Microbial isolation: cultured ~500 isolates from 50 traditional fermented foods (kimchi, miso, tempeh, kombucha, kefir) from diverse geographic sources.

updates.author: Mei-Ling Zhao & Lukas Bergström
updates.title: March Update: Field Testing Underway
updates.content:
We launched field testing of the Good Bug Bad Bug diagnostic protocol at 5 industrial fermentation facilities. The integrated diagnostic platform (E-nose + metabolomics + rapid sequencing) has been deployed at each site.

Initial results very promising: in 3 facilities, the system detected early contamination (Acetobacter and wild Lactobacillus) that culture methods missed until 48-72 hours later. Early detection enabled intervention—facilities were able to restart fermentations without significant product loss.

We're also refining the diagnostic algorithms based on real-world data. The machine learning models improve with each additional fermentation batch tested.

updates.author: Mei-Ling Zhao & Lukas Bergström
updates.title: December: Diagnostic Protocol v1.0 Complete
updates.content:
We completed the Good Bug Bad Bug diagnostic protocol v1.0. The platform integrates three complementary detection methods:

1. E-nose (volatiles): detects fermentation-associated vs. contamination-associated compounds
2. Targeted metabolomics (LC-MS): measures specific organic acids and flavor compounds indicating microbial metabolic state
3. Rapid 16S sequencing (Oxford MinION): provides definitive organism identification within 6-8 hours

Validation on 200 fermentation experiments (across 10 food types) showed:
- 98% sensitivity (true positive rate) for detecting pathogenic/spoilage organisms
- 99% specificity (true negative rate) for correctly identifying beneficial organisms
- Average time to identification: 8 hours vs. 7-14 days for culture methods

We filed a patent application covering the integrated diagnostic approach.

updates.author: Mei-Ling Zhao & Lukas Bergström
updates.title: August: Collaborative Research Begins
updates.content:
We officially began the Good Bug Bad Bug collaboration, leveraging complementary strengths: Zhao's fermentation microbiology expertise and Bergström's electronic nose technology.

We established a collaborative workspace and began designing the integrated diagnostic platform. Key insight: E-nose volatile fingerprints provide rapid initial screening; metabolomics adds biochemical confirmation; rapid sequencing provides definitive species identification.

We collected baseline data on 50 fermentation experiments and 30 microbial pure cultures to establish reference signatures for beneficial organisms (various Lactobacillus species) and contaminants (Listeria, wild yeasts, acetic acid bacteria).

feedback.author: Prof. Raj Kumar
feedback.title: Field testing results and diagnostic integration with Fermentation Whisperer
feedback.content:
The early-contamination detection results from the 5 industrial sites are very strong — catching Acetobacter 48–72 hours before culture methods is exactly the kind of practical impact EPSRC wants to see. A few suggestions:

The e-nose + metabolomics + sequencing pipeline is comprehensive but the 6–8 hour time-to-result is still too slow for some industrial use cases. Breweries making multiple batches per shift need answers in under 2 hours. Have you considered whether the e-nose alone (without sequencing confirmation) has sufficient specificity for a first-pass screening? If the false positive rate is below 5%, a two-tier system (rapid e-nose screen → confirmatory sequencing only for flagged batches) could be more practical.

Also worth connecting formally with Mei's Fermentation Whisperer monitoring dashboard. Her real-time sensor pipeline already ingests similar data streams — if the GBBB diagnostic model could run as a plugin within that dashboard, both projects benefit and the demo is much more compelling for the annual review.

projects.title: The Sustainable Kitchen: Energy-Optimised Hardware
projects.description: Designing cooking apparatus for minimal energy consumption without compromising technique or flavour.
projects.abstract: Cooking consumes substantial energy with significant environmental impact, yet many cooking techniques have not been optimized for efficiency. This project redesigns core cooking apparatus—ovens, burners, fryers, steamers—using principles of thermodynamic optimization and sensory science. We maintain organoleptic quality through improved heat distribution and closed-loop sensory control while reducing energy consumption by 30-50%. The hardware designs are combined with sustainable sourcing guidance and environmental impact assessment to create a complete framework for minimizing kitchen environmental footprint.

Central question: Can precision thermal control combining multiple heating modalities (induction + radiant + convection) with real-time sensory feedback achieve cuisine-quality cooking at 40-60% reduced energy input?

updates.author: Kwame Asante & Sofia Petridis
updates.title: March Update: Prototype Designs Attracting Industry Interest
updates.content:
Excellent progress on hardware designs. Our convection oven prototype is working beautifully—achieving 45% energy reduction while maintaining identical cooking performance (browning consistency, moisture loss). The improved heat distribution design is elegant and could be integrated into existing commercial oven designs.

The redesigned stovetop burner achieved 35% energy reduction via improved flame geometry and insulation. Sensory testing shows cooking outcomes (searing, simmering) are equivalent to standard burners.

We've received inquiries from 3 major commercial kitchen equipment manufacturers interested in licensing the designs. We're also preparing an Applied Energy paper on the thermodynamic optimization framework.

Next major challenge: the deep fryer. Oil heating is inherently inefficient; current prototypes show modest 15-20% improvements with additional R&D needed.

updates.author: Kwame Asante & Sofia Petridis
updates.title: November: Hardware Design Review Complete
updates.content:
We completed technical design review for three appliances: convection oven, stovetop burner, and steamer. Key design improvements:

1. Convection Oven: Multi-layer insulation, improved air circulation, heat recovery exchanger. Modeling predicts 45% energy reduction.
2. Burner: Optimized flame geometry, insulation collar, pre-heating chamber for air. Predicts 35% energy reduction.
3. Steamer: Pressure-assisted steaming with improved condensation recovery. Predicts 25% energy reduction.

We built working prototypes for oven and burner. Initial testing shows promising results matching modeling predictions. We're also conducting sensory testing to confirm cooking quality is maintained.

The collaboration between SousBot's sensory feedback expertise and Carbon Footprint's lifecycle thinking is proving very valuable.

updates.author: Kwame Asante & Sofia Petridis
updates.title: August: Energy Modeling and Design Framework
updates.content:
We completed the energy modeling framework for kitchen apparatus. We modeled thermal flows in typical cooking scenarios:
- Convection oven (roasting chicken, baking)
- Stovetop burner (simmering, searing, boiling)
- Deep fryer (temperature maintenance, cooking)
- Steamer (vegetable cooking, dumpling cooking)

Analysis revealed major inefficiencies:
- Ovens: 50-60% of heat lost through walls/door
- Burners: 30-40% of energy wasted as non-useful heat
- Fryers: 20-30% of energy for temperature maintenance

We identified key redesign opportunities: improved insulation, heat recovery, optimized heat distribution. Next phase: build prototypes and test sensory outcomes.

feedback.author: Prof. Eleanor Whitfield
feedback.title: Supplier situation and contingency planning
feedback.content:
The Hartfield supplier loss is concerning — this is the second hardware procurement setback in six months. A few things:

First, have we explored the University of Thornbridge's precision engineering workshop? They fabricated custom heating elements for the Materials Science department last year and the lead time was about 3 weeks. The tolerances may not match industrial spec but could be sufficient for prototype iteration. Worth a conversation with Dr. Parsons in Mechanical Engineering.

Second, the negative-energy vegan lasagne result is almost certainly the thermal recovery coefficient sign issue Hannah identified, but please do document it properly rather than just fixing the sign. If the model is sensitive enough to go negative from one coefficient flip, it may be sensitive to other small perturbations in ways we haven't tested. A brief sensitivity analysis would be worthwhile.

On the positive side, the 45% energy reduction figure is excellent and the Applied Energy paper should be strong. Make sure the comparison methodology is watertight — reviewers will scrutinise whether the sensory equivalence claim is properly controlled.

updates.author: Kwame Asante
updates.title: Idiom Pre-Filter Deployed; Grounding Error Rate Halved
updates.content:
We deployed the non-compositional idiom recogniser that Kwame proposed after the HRI workshop safety incident. The system now intercepts 152 cooking-specific idiomatic expressions before they reach the semantic parser.

The idiom list was compiled from three sources: (1) manual extraction from our 500k-recipe corpus (87 idioms), (2) a crowdsourced survey of 45 professional chefs across 6 cuisines (added 42 unique idioms), and (3) systematic mining of cooking forum posts for figurative language (added 23 more). Each idiom is mapped to a canonical action representation — e.g., 'take it off the heat' → `MOVE(object=pan, destination=cold_zone)`, 'knock back the dough' → `DEFLATE(object=dough, method=punch)`.

The pre-filter uses exact string matching with lemmatised variants plus a shallow neural classifier (fine-tuned DistilBERT) for compositional/non-compositional disambiguation. On a held-out test set of 500 cooking instructions (half literal, half idiomatic), the filter achieves:

- Idiom detection recall: 94%
- Idiom detection precision: 91%
- End-to-end action grounding accuracy: 93% (up from 87% pre-filter)
- Safety-critical misparses: 0 in 500 test cases (vs. 3 previously)

The remaining 6% missed idioms are mostly rare regional expressions ('give it laldy' — Scottish for vigorous stirring). We're expanding coverage iteratively as Kenji's dialect corpus grows.

Separately, we ran a small multilingual feasibility study: 200 French and 200 Japanese cooking instructions through the pipeline (with Google Translate as a preprocessing step). Action grounding accuracy drops to 71% (French) and 63% (Japanese), confirming that direct translation is insufficient — the idiomatic structure of cooking language is deeply language-specific. Proper multilingual support will require per-language idiom lists and culturally-aware action ontologies.

updates.author: Tomas Eriksson & Kwame Asante
updates.title: March: HRI Workshop Demonstration Success
updates.content:
We successfully demonstrated the SousBot Speaks system at the HRI 2026 workshop. The demo featured a live cooking task: chefs provided natural language instructions ("sear the steak until the surface is golden brown with slight char marks"), which the system parsed and executed on the SousBot hardware.

The demo was very well-received. Average first-attempt success rate: 87% (10 trials with 8 different chefs providing varied instruction styles). Failures were typically due to ambiguous language that even humans would find ambiguous.

We received several invitations for follow-up collaborations from robotics labs and culinary institutions. We're preparing an NLP for Food workshop paper on the lessons learned.

updates.author: Tomas Eriksson & Kwame Asante
updates.title: November: NLP Model Training Complete
updates.content:
We completed training the core NLP model for cooking instruction understanding. The model was trained on:
- 500k+ recipes from multiple online sources
- 50k annotated cooking instruction sequences
- Culinary literature and cookbooks (processed via OCR)
- 100+ videos of cooking instructions (transcribed and annotated)

The trained model achieves:
- 91% accuracy on parsing cooking instructions into command sequences
- 88% semantic understanding of doneness descriptors ("rare", "medium-rare", "golden brown", etc.)
- 85% correct interpretation of ambiguous technique descriptions

We also created a semantic knowledge base of cooking concepts: techniques, ingredient states, cooking outcomes. This knowledge base feeds into the command generation system.

updates.author: Tomas Eriksson & Kwame Asante
updates.title: August: Project Kickoff and Data Collection
updates.content:
We officially started the SousBot Speaks collaboration. The vision: chefs and home cooks should be able to control autonomous cooking robots using natural language rather than formal programming.

We began comprehensive data collection:
- Mining 500k+ recipes for cooking instructions
- Annotating 2k sample instructions with semantic structure
- Collecting video cooking demonstrations from professional chefs
- Building a culinary semantic knowledge base

We also surveyed 30+ professional chefs and home cooks on their desired interface for cooking robots. Strong consensus: natural language would dramatically improve accessibility and usability.

Next phase: train NLP models on collected data.

currentChallenges.description: Voice interface still interprets "take it off the heat" as a request to physically remove the pan from the hob and hold it aloft. Safety review ongoing.

responses.author: kwame
responses.content: Resolved by the idiom pre-filter (see April update). 'Take it off the heat' now correctly maps to MOVE(object=pan, destination=cold_zone). The safety review is cleared — we ran 200 stress tests with adversarial phrasing and zero safety-critical misparses. Downgrading from blocking.

currentChallenges.description: Dialect coverage remains patchy for regional idioms; the model currently thinks "give it a wee toast" is emotional encouragement rather than a browning instruction.

responses.author: kenji
responses.content: Started building a regional cooking dialect corpus. Currently covering Scottish English (48 expressions), American Southern (35), and Australian (22). Each entry includes the regional phrase, standard English equivalent, and canonical action mapping. The DistilBERT classifier generalises reasonably to unseen expressions from covered dialects (~80% accuracy) but fails on uncovered ones. This is a long-tail problem — pragmatically, we'll focus on the top 5 English dialects by recipe corpus frequency and flag the rest for human review.

resolvedChallenges.description: Seq2seq model hallucinating cooking steps not present in the input recipe — generating phantom 'rest for 10 minutes' steps between every action, tripling estimated cook times.
resolvedChallenges.resolutionNote: The hallucinated rest steps were an artefact of the training data distribution — 60% of annotated recipes included explicit rest/cooling steps, biasing the decoder. Fixed by (1) rebalancing the training set to match natural recipe distributions, (2) adding a copy mechanism that anchors generated steps to spans in the input text, and (3) introducing a step-count loss term penalising outputs that exceed the input step count by >20%. Hallucination rate dropped from 34% to 3% of generated cooking plans.

feedback.author: Dr. Kwame Asante
feedback.title: Safety review and the 'take it off the heat' problem
feedback.content:
The HRI workshop demo was a success but the 'take it off the heat' safety issue needs resolving before any further live demos. The core problem is that the parser is treating idiomatic phrases as compositional — decomposing 'take off' into a physical lifting action. We need a non-compositional idiom recogniser that fires before the semantic parser.

I've started compiling a list of cooking-specific idioms from our recipe corpus. There are about 150 that have non-literal meanings ('bring to the boil', 'knock back the dough', 'fold in gently'). Tomas and I will build a pattern-matching pre-filter that catches these before they reach the action planner.

The dialect issue is lower priority but Kenji's right that it limits our claim of generalisability. For the NLP workshop paper, let's be honest about the English-centric limitation and frame multilingual support as future work.

projects.title: Terroir 2.0: Environment-Microbiome-Flavour Interactions
projects.description: Holistic computational model of how soil, climate, and microbial communities shape food flavour profiles.
projects.abstract: Terroir—the influence of environmental factors on food characteristics—is traditionally understood qualitatively. This project creates the first mechanistic, quantitative model of how soil chemistry, climate variables, and associated microbial communities shape flavour compound production in food crops. By integrating soil metagenomic data, climate measurements, plant transcriptomics, and sensory characterization, we model the complete environmental→genetic→biochemical→sensory pathway. The resulting framework enables prediction of crop characteristics from environmental conditions and identification of optimal growing conditions for target flavor profiles.

slides.title: Research Question & Background

updates.author: Priya Ramanathan
updates.title: Pilot Sampling at Côte de Nuits: Field Protocol and Preliminary 16S Results
updates.content:
## Field campaign

We completed a 5-day pilot sampling campaign at four vineyard plots in the Côte de Nuits (Gevrey-Chambertin, Morey-Saint-Denis, Chambolle-Musigny, Vougeot). These sites were selected because they span a well-characterised limestone–marl gradient over <8 km, with documented differences in wine character despite near-identical climate exposure. Each plot was sampled at three depths (0–10 cm, 10–30 cm, 30–60 cm) in triplicate, yielding 36 soil cores.

Grapevine root samples (fine roots, <2 mm diameter) were collected from 3 vines per plot for rhizosphere and endosphere fractionation. Grape bud samples were also taken — it is early in the season, but we want baseline metabolomic profiles before véraison.

All samples are now at Thornbridge for DNA extraction. Mei's lab is handling 16S and shotgun metagenomics; Ravi's group will do the root transcriptomics once we have RNA quality confirmed.

## Preliminary 16S from pilot

We fast-tracked 16S amplicon sequencing on the 12 surface-layer (0–10 cm) samples to test our extraction and bioinformatics pipeline. Results are encouraging:

- **Alpha diversity** (Shannon $H'$) ranges from 5.8 to 7.2 across the four sites — a wider spread than expected for sites this geographically close
- The Gevrey-Chambertin plot shows markedly higher Actinobacteria relative abundance ($31 \pm 4\%$) compared to the other three sites ($18–22\%$), which is interesting because Actinobacteria are associated with mineral nutrient cycling and antibiotic production in the rhizosphere
- UniFrac $\beta$-diversity analysis cleanly separates the four sites on PC1 (explaining $42\%$ of variance), which is a good sign — if sites were not distinguishable at the microbial level, the whole premise would be shaky

These are only surface-layer samples from a single timepoint, so we should not over-interpret. But they confirm the pipeline works end-to-end and that microbial community structure varies meaningfully across our study gradient.

## Data infrastructure

Nina has set up the shared data repository on the Thornbridge research data platform. The schema accommodates soil chemistry, 16S/metagenomic profiles, metabolomics, transcriptomics, climate logger data, and sensory panel scores — all linked by a site × timepoint × depth key. We are using the ISA-Tab metadata standard, which is standard in multi-omics studies but new territory for some of the team.

## What is not working yet

The cross-institutional data sharing agreement between Thornbridge and Lakemere is still in draft. Legal teams are negotiating IP terms around the predictive models — specifically, whether a trained model constitutes derived data or a new invention. This is blocking Mei from uploading her existing pilot fermentation data (from Fermentation Whisperer) that we planned to use for methods benchmarking. Amara is escalating through the PVC-Research office.

## Next steps

- Complete DNA extraction and submit full 36-sample 16S + shotgun libraries (target: mid-April)
- Install climate data loggers at all four pilot sites
- Finalise the sensory evaluation protocol with the Burgundy Institute partner (Prof. Dubois's group)
- Resolve the data sharing agreement (target: end of April)

updates.author: Priya Ramanathan, Mei-Ling Zhao, Ravi Chandra
updates.title: March Team Assembly and Project Planning
updates.content:
We held the kickoff meeting for the major Terroir 2.0 collaborative project ($2.1M HEFGA Frontier Research award). The core team brings together complementary expertise:

- Priya Ramanathan (topological modeling of flavor space)
- Mei-Ling Zhao (fermentation microbiology and metabolomics)
- Ravi Chandra (plant genetics and flavor engineering)
- Additional collaborators from soil science, climate modeling, and sensory science

We've identified initial study sites: 20 cacao and coffee plantations across diverse agro-climatic regions. We're establishing sample collection protocols (soil microbiome, plant tissues, flavor analysis) and beginning the massive data integration work.

The ambition is clear: create the first quantitative, mechanistic model of terroir. This will require unprecedented integration of environmental, microbiological, genomic, and sensory data.

feedback.author: Prof. Fiona McAllister
feedback.title: Thoughts on sequencing depth and the Actinobacteria signal
feedback.content:
Good to see the pilot pipeline working. Two notes:

The Actinobacteria enrichment at Gevrey-Chambertin is worth pursuing carefully. Streptomyces species in that phylum produce geosmin — the compound responsible for 'earthy' aroma in both soil and wine. If the enrichment is real and not a primer bias artefact, it could be a direct mechanistic link between soil microbiota and a sensory descriptor that sommeliers already use for that appellation. Worth running the same samples through our ITS2 primer set as well to check whether fungal communities (particularly mycorrhizal networks) co-vary.

On sequencing depth: 16S at the resolution you're running (V3–V4, ~20k reads per sample) will miss rare taxa that might still be functionally important. For the full 36-sample run, I'd recommend aiming for 50k+ reads and including some spike-in controls so we can estimate absolute abundances rather than just relative. Happy to advise on the spike-in protocol — we've optimised one for soil matrices.

publications.title: Personalised Nutrition Algorithms: From Genetics to Plate

conceptNotes.title: Taste Perception Under Microgravity: Implications for Space Gastronomy
conceptNotes.rationale: The altered taste perception experienced by astronauts in microgravity presents a unique opportunity to decouple olfactory and taste pathways from proprioceptive feedback. This proposal explores whether computational flavour adjustment algorithms could compensate for astronauts' diminished taste acuity, enabling more enjoyable meals during long-duration space missions.
conceptNotes.relevance: Directly complements FlavorSpace's topological perception modelling by testing predictions in extreme sensory environments. Results may reveal fundamental principles of taste perception across different vestibular states.
conceptNotes.preliminaryInsights: Literature review indicates ~70% of astronauts report taste suppression due to nasal congestion and fluid redistribution. Preliminary analysis suggests targeted volatilization might restore perceptual resolution.
conceptNotes.nextSteps: Secure partnership with space agencies or parabolic flight programs. Design controlled tasting panels during brief microgravity exposure (~25 seconds per flight). Collect pilot data on 6-8 trained tasters.

conceptNotes.title: Adversarial Recipes: Can GANs Generate Dishes That Fool Trained Sommeliers?
conceptNotes.rationale: Generative Adversarial Networks (GANs) have revolutionized image synthesis and text generation. This proposal extends adversarial methods to recipe generation: can a GAN produce dishes that expert sommeliers cannot distinguish from human-created recipes, and what do the "adversarial recipes" reveal about implicit culinary principles?
conceptNotes.relevance: Complements RecipeGraph by introducing adversarial learning to culinary reasoning. Success would validate that our knowledge graph embeddings capture true culinary semantics rather than surface correlations.
conceptNotes.preliminaryInsights: Initial experiments with a variational autoencoder (VAE) on 50k recipes show promise—the latent space separates cuisines and cooking methods meaningfully. Preliminary GAN architectures are now in training.
conceptNotes.nextSteps: Train conditional GAN on full 500k recipe corpus. Recruit expert chef panel (n=12) for blind taste-test validation. Publish adversarial recipes and expert confusion matrices.

conceptNotes.title: The Maillard Reaction as a Turing-Complete Process
conceptNotes.rationale: The Maillard reaction—non-enzymatic browning via amino acid-reducing sugar condensation—occurs across a vast parameter space (temperature, pH, moisture, time). This theoretical proposal argues that the reaction's outputs (flavour compounds, browning intensity, texture change) can encode arbitrary computational information, potentially supporting universal computation in chemical systems.
conceptNotes.relevance: Extends the programme's computational gastronomy mandate by demonstrating that food chemistry itself may instantiate computation. Provides theoretical foundation for "cooking as computation" frameworks.
conceptNotes.preliminaryInsights: Preliminary thermodynamic analysis suggests the reaction exhibits sufficient degeneracy and feedback loops to emulate Boolean logic gates. Proof-of-concept: encoding binary digits via sugar-amino acid ratios in test tubes (under review).
conceptNotes.nextSteps: Complete formal proof that Maillard reaction trajectories can compute any Turing machine. Validate with wet-lab experiments encoding a simple algorithm (e.g., binary addition). Aim for theoretical computer science publication.

progressSignals.note: Taken forward as a theoretical strand within fermentation work.

conceptNotes.title: Sourdough Starter as Distributed Biological Computer
conceptNotes.rationale: Sourdough fermentation involves dynamic microbial consortia (Lactobacillus, Saccharomyces) exhibiting complex chemical signalling and metabolic interdependencies. We propose modeling sourdough starters as distributed biological computers, where individual microbial cells perform local computations and propagate results through metabolic byproducts (organic acids, volatiles, CO2).
conceptNotes.relevance: Bridges microbial ecology and computational theory. Findings could inform both fermentation control strategies and our understanding of information processing in biological systems.
conceptNotes.preliminaryInsights: Transcriptomics of lab-maintained starters reveals time-varying gene expression patterns consistent with feedback oscillators. Metabolomics data show synchronized organic acid production suggesting coordinated metabolic computation.
conceptNotes.nextSteps: Build computational model (ODEs) of metabolic cross-talk in starter consortia. Validate predictions with continuous fermentation bioreactor experiments. Test whether starter "computes" optimal dough acidity and gas production.

conceptNotes.title: Umami Perception Biomarkers: A Genetic and Neuroimaging Study
conceptNotes.rationale: Umami perception varies dramatically between individuals—some people find MSG delicious, others detect little flavour. This proposal seeks genetic markers (taste receptor variants, olfactory SNPs) and neuroimaging correlates (fMRI activation in taste cortex) underlying individual differences in umami detection threshold and hedonic response.
conceptNotes.relevance: Supports Hannah's personalised nutrition programme by identifying umami responsiveness as a genotype-phenotype trait. Results will inform tailored dietary recommendations.
conceptNotes.preliminaryInsights: Preliminary analysis of existing taste genetics databases shows TAS1R3 and TRPM5 variants correlating with umami detection sensitivity. fMRI data from 25 subjects shows insula and orbitofrontal cortex involvement.
conceptNotes.nextSteps: Recruit and genotype n=100 subjects. Conduct fMRI during umami tasting, collect behavioral thresholds. Publish GWAS results and fMRI-behavior associations.

conceptNotes.title: Machine Learning for Predicting Crop Flavour Traits from Genomic Data
conceptNotes.rationale: Modern crop breeding selects for yield, disease resistance, and shelf-life but largely ignores flavour. This proposal develops ML models predicting flavour compound profiles (terpenoids, esters, thiols) directly from genomic data, enabling flavour-focused crop improvement and accelerating breeding cycles.
conceptNotes.relevance: Unifies agricultural genomics and computational flavor science. Could enable rapid development of superior-tasting heritage crop varieties, supporting food quality and consumer satisfaction.
conceptNotes.preliminaryInsights: Using XGBoost on existing GWAS data from heritage tomato accessions, achieved R² = 0.68 predicting total volatile content. Feature importance analysis highlights key flavour loci.
conceptNotes.nextSteps: Expand to 15 crop species. Validate predictions experimentally by growing predicted high-flavour genotypes. Partner with seed companies for breeding pipeline integration.

progressSignals.note: Connected breeding and recommendation work around shared flavour loci.

conceptNotes.title: Temporal Dynamics of Flavour Compound Release During Cooking: A Multi-Modal Sensor Network
conceptNotes.rationale: Flavour compound release during cooking is a dynamic process—volatile concentrations peak, plateau, and decay over minutes to hours. Traditional snapshots (single GC-MS measurement) miss temporal evolution. This proposal deploys a network of electronic nose sensors coupled with temporal GC-MS sampling to characterize compound volatilization kinetics across diverse cooking methods.
conceptNotes.relevance: Supports SousBot, RecipeGraph, and FlavorSpace by providing rich temporal data on how cooking transforms ingredient chemistry into perceived flavour. Enables computational modelling of flavour development.
conceptNotes.preliminaryInsights: Pilot study with bread baking shows clear temporal phases: ester formation (0-10 min), Maillard peak (10-25 min), volatilization plateau (25+ min). Sensor signal tracking is promising.
conceptNotes.nextSteps: Deploy sensor network in test kitchen. Collect temporal profiles for 20 cooking protocols (roasting, boiling, frying, sous-vide). Build kinetic models predicting flavour trajectory.

conceptNotes.title: Blockchain for Food Supply Chain Transparency: Flavor Provenance and Authenticity
conceptNotes.rationale: Consumer interest in food origins, farming practices, and authenticity is rising. This proposal explores blockchain-based supply chain tracking linking farm metadata (soil type, climate, cultivation practices) to final product chemistry (volatile profiles, isotope ratios) to enable consumers to verify flavour provenance and detect adulteration.
conceptNotes.relevance: Addresses sustainability and consumer trust themes. Supports Terroir 2.0 by providing cryptographic provenance for regional food characteristics. Could differentiate premium products in marketplace.
conceptNotes.preliminaryInsights: Prototype blockchain schema designed storing farm data, harvest dates, processing steps, and isotope signatures. Preliminary validation on regional tomato supply chain shows ~85% traceability coverage.
conceptNotes.nextSteps: Expand pilot to 5 supply chains (olive oil, wine, coffee, chocolate, honey). Integrate ML models predicting expected flavour profile from provenance data. Conduct consumer validation studies.

conceptNotes.title: Aji Amarillo Lines for High-Volatile Sauce Bases
conceptNotes.rationale: Aji Amarillo pepper lines sit at a useful junction between flavour engineering and downstream culinary use. A small programme pilot could test whether volatile-rich breeding lines produce more distinctive sauce bases and whether that signal is strong enough to matter for recommendation systems.
conceptNotes.relevance: Connects Genome to Gastronome and CropToPlate with a concrete cultivar, a manageable scope, and a clear route from breeding data to recipe behaviour.
conceptNotes.preliminaryInsights: Existing pepper genotype and volatile data already cover enough promising material to support a narrow pilot without standing up a new data collection effort first.
conceptNotes.nextSteps: Agree whether this should remain in active view, become a small joint pilot this summer, or be folded into ongoing crop-flavour work.

progressSignals.note: Used in crop-flavour discussion about a focused summer pilot.
